reviewedBy: implementation workers for the manipulation, classical and rl-sim2real humanize passes of 2026-10-12, combined into one review by the integration lane (not independent acceptance)
ownerApproval: Josef, 12 Oct 2026: "ensure we remove AI slop etc and keep it extremely premium. not too long text." The humanize lane's length decision of the same day, recorded for Josef, authorizes cutting recap paragraphs, repeated numbers, secondary corroboration and minor reporting caveats, keeps every caveat whose removal would overstate a result and at least 30 cited sources per article, and approves dropped numbers, recap citations, successor reviews of the older continuity records and retired or moved phrase pins. Not release approval. Additions: the owner-proxy directive of 2026-10-21 03:40 (owner-decision-kol-batch-next-dispatch-20261020, under owner-decision-kol-backlog-batch-20260930 and owner-decision-kol-coverage-and-evidence-standards-20260924) admits attributed, dated KOL paragraphs, each claim checked against its primary source, onto these articles; each is recorded here as added occurrences and registered in the deltas ledger.
rationale: The owner asked for short, premium articles. A cut to about a quarter less text must drop recap paragraphs, numbers stated twice, secondary examples and minor reporting caveats, which the word-budget trim cannot admit because it keeps every number, citation and link in place. This review records each such cut as exact edits over the bytes the article had before it, lists every citation, number, link and glossary occurrence that left the body with the sentence it came from, and lists the test pins the cut retired or moved. The earlier bytes stand in for the live article only while the live article is exactly the reviewed successor, so older reviews, runs and receipts that pinned the earlier bytes still check the bytes they recorded. A later reviewed addition is recorded in the same review: every citation, number, link and glossary occurrence it brings into the body is listed under added with the sentence it went into, its new sources are appended to the frontmatter citations list, and the body stays shorter than it was before the cut.

edits.before: Intrinsics map pixels to rays through focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's method recovers them from a planar pattern seen at a few unknown orientations, with a closed-form solution and nonlinear refinement <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />. Kannala and Brandt's generic model covers conventional, wide-angle and fisheye lenses <Cite id="kannala-brandt-2006" />. AnyCalib estimates intrinsics from one in-the-wild image for pinhole, Brown-Conrady and Kannala-Brandt models <Cite id="anycalib-2025" />. Refit them after any focus, resolution or crop change.

edits.before: Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />. Tsai and Lenz's solution takes about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations, and a few milliseconds <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />. Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions on the Euclidean group <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />, and Daniilidis solved rotation and translation together with dual quaternions <Cite id="daniilidis-1999" />. AprilTag targets give a full 6-DoF pose from one image <Cite id="apriltag-2011" />.
edits.after: Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />, Tsai and Lenz solved it in about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />, and Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />.

DRHeC's authors report 88.9% grasp success on a UR5e, 46.3 points above EasyHeC <Cite id="drhec-2026" />.
edits.after: Markerless methods now rival targets: DREAM's single-image accuracy is comparable to multi-frame offline calibration <Cite id="dream-2019" />, and Hydra reaches 5 mm task-space accuracy against 7 mm for classical methods <Cite id="hydra-hand-eye-2025" />. edits.before: Control is the use of feedback to make a robot follow a reference, such as a [motion plan](/classical/motion-planning), despite model error and disturbances: measure the state, compare it with the reference, and correct <Cite id="fbs-2020" />. Loops run at every level, from motor drivers to whole-body torque control, beneath any learned policy.
edits.after: Control uses feedback to make a robot follow a reference, such as a [motion plan](/classical/motion-planning), despite model error and disturbances: measure the state, compare it with the reference, correct <Cite id="fbs-2020" />. Feedback loops run beneath any learned policy, from motor drivers to whole-body torque control.

edits.after: For an error $e(t) = r(t) - y(t)$ between reference and measured output, a PID controller commands <Cite id="fbs-2020" />

edits.before: Ziegler and Nichols described proportional response as valve movement proportional to the measured displacement, automatic reset as movement that eliminates a sustained offset, and pre-act as movement proportional to the rate of pen movement. These are the proportional, integral and derivative actions. Their 1942 tuning rules drive the loop into oscillation with proportional gain alone, then back off from the critical gain and period by fixed fractions <Cite id="ziegler-nichols-1942" />.
edits.after: Ziegler and Nichols called the three actions proportional response, automatic reset and pre-act. Their 1942 tuning rules drive the loop into oscillation with proportional gain alone, then back off from the critical gain and period by fixed fractions <Cite id="ziegler-nichols-1942" />.

edits.before: Integral action gives zero steady-state error, so it removes the offset a constant disturbance leaves under proportional control. Under actuator saturation it needs anti-windup compensation to avoid integrator windup. Åström and Murray quote a survey in which 97% of over eleven thousand regulatory controllers in refining, chemicals and pulp and paper used PID <Cite id="fbs-2020" />.
edits.after: Integral action removes the steady-state offset that a constant disturbance leaves under proportional control, and it needs anti-windup when the actuator saturates. Åström and Murray quote a survey in which 97% of over eleven thousand regulatory controllers in refining, chemicals and pulp and paper used PID <Cite id="fbs-2020" />.

edits.before: MPC grew out of 1970s and 1980s power-plant and refinery practice, where slow, constrained, multivariable plants defeated PID <Cite id="garcia-1989" /><Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. A mid-1999 vendor survey counted more than 4,600 applications, concentrated in refining and petrochemicals <Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. Di Carlo and colleagues ran convex MPC on the MIT Cheetah 3 as a single rigid body with contact forces as decision variables. Horizons reached half a second, each QP took under a millisecond at 20 to 30 Hz, and one gain set served every gait from standing to gallop <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />.
edits.after: MPC grew out of 1970s and 1980s power-plant and refinery practice, where slow, constrained, multivariable plants defeated PID <Cite id="garcia-1989" /><Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. On the MIT Cheetah 3, Di Carlo and colleagues' convex MPC solved each QP in under a millisecond at 20 to 30 Hz, and one gain set served every gait from standing to gallop <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />.

edits.before: Full-order MPC has run on legged hardware for a decade. Koenemann and colleagues applied whole-body MPC in real time on the HRP-2 humanoid in 2015, the first such controller on a complex dynamic robot by their account <Cite id="koenemann-2015" />. Neunert and colleagues ran whole-body nonlinear MPC through contacts on a quadruped at up to 190 Hz with a half-second horizon <Cite id="neunert-2018" />. DIAL-MPC optimizes full-order quadruped dynamics in real time without training and beats RL policies by 50% on climbing tasks <Cite id="dial-mpc-2024" />. Zhang and colleagues offer an easy-to-reproduce baseline: iLQR with MuJoCo dynamics and finite-difference derivatives, running whole-body MPC on quadrupeds and a full-sized humanoid with few sim-to-real considerations <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />. [Reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) compares it with learned policies.
edits.after: On legged hardware, DIAL-MPC optimizes full-order quadruped dynamics in real time without training and beats RL policies by 50% on climbing tasks <Cite id="dial-mpc-2024" />. [Reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) compares these controllers with learned policies.

edits.before: Its variables are joint accelerations, torques and contact forces, its equality constraint is the rigid-body dynamics, and $\mathcal{F}$ holds the friction cones. Each task, such as torso posture or swing-foot tracking, is a weighted row of the objective. Kuindersma and colleagues built Atlas's controller from convex, mixed-integer and sparse nonlinear optimization, from footstep placement to whole-body control <Cite id="kuindersma-2015" />.
edits.after: Its variables are joint accelerations, torques and contact forces; the rigid-body dynamics are the equality constraint, $\mathcal{F}$ holds the friction cones, and each task is one weighted row of the objective.

edits.before: In contact, a stiff position-controlled arm driven into a surface 2 mm nearer than modeled turns position error into stored collision energy. Hogan's 1985 <Term id="impedance-control">impedance control</Term> commands the relationship between force and motion instead, so the manipulator presents a programmable mass-spring-damper to the environment. A contact is an interaction port with force and velocity as conjugate variables: a controller commands one, and the environment fixes the other <Cite id="hogan-1985" />.
edits.after: A stiff position-controlled arm driven into a surface 2 mm nearer than modeled turns that error into stored collision energy. Hogan's 1985 <Term id="impedance-control">impedance control</Term> instead commands the relationship between force and motion, so the arm presents a programmable mass-spring-damper: at a contact, a controller commands force or velocity, and the environment fixes the other <Cite id="hogan-1985" />.

edits.before: Salisbury's active stiffness control, five years earlier, set the apparent Cartesian stiffness per task axis <Cite id="salisbury-1980" />. <Term id="admittance-control">Admittance control</Term> is the dual: measure force with a wrist sensor and command motion. A backdrivable direct-drive arm realizes an impedance directly, while a stiff geared arm with a force-torque sensor runs admittance in software. Ott, Mukherjee and Nakamura's unified formulation treats the two as one port with flipped causality and gives stability conditions for switching and interpolating between them <Cite id="ott-2010" />.
edits.after: <Term id="admittance-control">Admittance control</Term> is the dual: measure force with a wrist sensor and command motion. A backdrivable direct-drive arm realizes an impedance directly, while a stiff geared arm with a force-torque sensor runs admittance in software.

edits.before: Mason's and Raibert and Craig's <Term id="hybrid-force-position-control">hybrid force/position control</Term> splits the contact into a task frame from its geometry. It controls force along the constrained axes and position along the free ones, never both on one axis <Cite id="mason-1981" /> <Cite id="raibert-craig-1981" />. Polishing controls force normal to the surface and position along it; the contact geometry must be known in advance.
edits.after: Mason's and Raibert and Craig's <Term id="hybrid-force-position-control">hybrid force/position control</Term> builds a task frame from the contact geometry and controls force along the constrained axes and position along the free ones, never both on one axis <Cite id="mason-1981" /> <Cite id="raibert-craig-1981" />. Polishing, for instance, controls force normal to the surface and position along it, which needs the contact geometry in advance.

edits.before: Learned policies now set impedance. Adaptive Compliance Policy learns spatially and temporally varying compliance from human demonstrations and reports over 50% improvement over state-of-the-art visuomotor policies <Cite id="acp-2024" />. A diffusion-based impedance learner co-authored by Hogan adapts stiffness and damping online on a torque-controlled KUKA LBR iiwa and reached 100% success in multi-geometry peg-in-hole insertion <Cite id="geiger-impedance-2025" />. Intrinsic, which ran the 2026 AI for Industry Challenge, reports that 90% of the top teams in its real-workcell phase inserted the connector with rules-based routines such as spiral searches, using force-torque feedback <Cite id="intrinsic-ai-for-industry-challenge-2026" />.
edits.after: Learned policies now set impedance: Adaptive Compliance Policy learns spatially and temporally varying compliance from human demonstrations and reports over 50% improvement over state-of-the-art visuomotor policies <Cite id="acp-2024" />. A diffusion-based impedance learner co-authored by Hogan adapts stiffness and damping online on a torque-controlled KUKA LBR iiwa <Cite id="geiger-impedance-2025" />. Intrinsic, which ran the 2026 AI for Industry Challenge, reports that 90% of the top teams in its real-workcell phase inserted the connector with rules-based routines, such as spiral searches, and force-torque feedback <Cite id="intrinsic-ai-for-industry-challenge-2026" />.

edits.before: A position-controlled, non-backdrivable geared arm without a force sensor has no force channel. Position error, gear ratio and the surface set the contact force, so a joint-position policy on it cannot regulate force in the contact-rich tasks of [dexterity](/frontier/dexterity). <Term id="series-elastic-actuator">Series elastic actuation</Term> puts a deliberate spring in the actuator for shock tolerance and more accurate, stable force control <Cite id="pratt-williamson-1995" />. Ott, Albu-Schäffer and colleagues based Cartesian impedance control of flexible-joint robots on exact torque decoupling, with a stability proof and a single-joint test <Cite id="albu-schaffer-2003" />. Franka's interface exposes a 1 kHz torque-level layer with Cartesian impedance controllers <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />, while Universal Robots' URScript force mode takes a task frame, compliant axes, target forces and position-deviation limits <Cite id="ur-force-mode-docs" />. <Term id="backdrivability">Backdrivability</Term> is an actuator decision that fixes which schemes the hardware can attempt.
edits.after:
A non-backdrivable, position-controlled geared arm without a force sensor has no force channel: position error, gear ratio and the surface set the contact force, so a joint-position policy on it cannot regulate force in the contact-rich tasks of [dexterity](/frontier/dexterity). <Term id="series-elastic-actuator">Series elastic actuation</Term> adds a deliberate spring for shock tolerance and more accurate, stable force control <Cite id="pratt-williamson-1995" />.

Franka's interface exposes a 1 kHz torque-level layer with Cartesian impedance controllers <Cite id="franka-fci-docs" />, while Universal Robots' URScript force mode takes a task frame, compliant axes, target forces and position-deviation limits <Cite id="ur-force-mode-docs" />. <Term id="backdrivability">Backdrivability</Term> is an actuator decision that fixes which of these schemes the hardware can attempt.

edits.before: The contact lab's transient force limit comes from published biomechanical measurements <Cite id="han-force-pain-2024" />. ISO/TS 15066:2016 holds the original collaborative-robot tables <Cite id="iso-ts-15066" />. edits.before: Shrinking the robot to a point and growing each obstacle by its shape reduces collision checking to point membership. Planning becomes the search for a continuous curve in $\mathcal{C}_{free}$ from $q_{start}$ to $q_{goal}$ <Cite id="lozano-perez-1983" />. Explicit boundary or solid models of $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ are difficult to build, though semi-algebraic models for chains and trees can be generated automatically. The basic semi-algebraic mover problem is PSPACE-hard when the number of <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">degrees of freedom</Term> is unbounded <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. Hardness holds for a planar linkage with multiple links and for a multi-arm robot among 3D polyhedra; Canny's roadmap method is singly exponential <Cite id="solovey-complexity-2020" />.

OMPL 2.0 targets real-time planning through hardware acceleration <Cite id="ompl-2-2026" />; release 2.0.0 of April 6, 2026 added VAMP as a SIMD backend, reaching planning speeds up to 25 kHz <Cite id="ompl-release-notes-2026" />. This prolate hyperspheroid has the start and goal as foci and the best path length $c_{best}$ as transverse diameter. It contains every state on a strictly improving path, but its states need not be collision-free, so collision checks remain. Over 100 runs per variation with 60 seconds of refinement, it refined faster than RRT\*, and it gains nothing once the set covers the domain <Cite id="gammell-2014" />.

FMT\* gave the first convergence-rate bounds in optimal sampling-based planning <Cite id="fmt-star-2013" />. BIT\* orders its search by potential solution quality, as in A\*, and keeps improving with more time, as in RRT\* <Cite id="bit-star-2017" />. AORRTC finds first solutions as fast as RRT-Connect, then converges. It solves difficult high-DoF problems in milliseconds where other almost-surely asymptotically optimal planners failed to find solutions consistently within seconds <Cite id="aorrtc-2025" />.

On LittleDog it ran inside a footstep controller with a separate footstep planner and a ZMP preview controller seeding the trunk. edits.before: Waypoint checks can miss collisions between waypoints, so TrajOpt penalizes a swept volume: the convex hull of endpoint shapes, inflated for rotation. The rotation bound adds $d_{\mathrm{arc}}=r\phi^2/8$ to the safety margin, a correction omitted in experiments because it was well under 1 cm. The swept-volume gradient is not guaranteed accurate in 3D. The implementation used Bullet with convex hulls of robot meshes and penalized self-collisions only at discrete times <Cite id="schulman-2013" />. The 2014 journal version covers 7-DoF arms, 18-DoF full-body robots, statically stable walking for the 34-DoF Atlas humanoid and physical experiments with the 18-DoF PR2 <Cite id="trajopt-ijrr-2014" />.

Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion. edits.before: Stereo triangulates features matched between two images, so a featureless surface gives it nothing to match. Intel's RGBD depth cameras add an active texture projector, a technique classical stereo used as far back as 1984, to generate texture that makes matching unambiguous <Cite id="keselman-2017-realsense" />. The March 2026 RealSense D400 datasheet lists ±2% Z-accuracy up to 2 m for D410/D415 and D43x, over an 80% region of interest at HD resolution. Range limits differ by model: up to 4 m for D450/D455/D455f/D456 and 0.5 m for D401/D405. Accuracy compares valid pixels with ground truth over 80% of the depth field of view, and factory KPIs reflect typical conditions. The D405 is tested on a textured target in about 250 lux room light, the others on a texture-less white target at the default 150 mW laser power and auto exposure <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. RealSense has been independent of Intel since 11 July 2025 <Cite id="realsense-spinout-2025" />.

- Transparent surfaces refract light, so the sensor ranges whatever lies behind them. ClearGrasp starts from the observation that transparent objects "often appear as noisy or distorted approximations of the surfaces that lie behind them". It infers surface normals, transparent-surface masks and occlusion boundaries, then *replaces* the returned depth <Cite id="cleargrasp-2020" />. TransCG supplies 57,715 real RGB-D images from 130 scenes for transparent-object depth completion <Cite id="transcg-2022" />.
- Specular reflections can saturate D400 images, while the D400f column says "Saturation mitigated" <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. Azure Kinect lists saturated IR signal as its own invalidation cause <Cite id="azure-kinect-depth-docs-2026" />. DREDS simulates an active stereo sensor over 130K photorealistic images, and a restoration network trained on it generalizes to real depth datasets such as ClearGrasp's <Cite id="dreds-2022" />.

edits.before: In SAM's single-point test across 23 datasets, the prompt is the ground-truth mask's center and the output SAM's most confident mask, which beats RITM's mIoU on 16. Free-form text was a separately trained, CLIP-conditioned proof of concept, and the geometric-prompt model has no demonstrated text capability. Fine structures and boundaries remain failure cases. The prompt step of about 50 ms on a browser CPU assumes a precomputed embedding, and the heavy image encoder prevents overall real-time performance <Cite id="segment-anything-2023" />. SAM 3 (2025) takes concept prompts, short noun phrases or image exemplars, and returns masks and identities for every matching instance. Its data engine produced 4M unique concept labels, and its authors report doubling the accuracy of existing systems on image and video concept segmentation <Cite id="sam3-2025" />.
edits.after: SAM 2 extends prompting to video with a streaming memory of earlier predictions and prompted frames. Objects are inferred independently, and failures persist after shot changes or long occlusions, in crowded scenes and on thin, fast-moving details <Cite id="sam2-2024" />.

Grounded SAM feeds Grounding DINO's open-set boxes to SAM and reports 48.7 mean AP on the zero-shot SegInW benchmark <Cite id="grounded-sam-2024" />. CNOS segments unseen objects by matching DINOv2 descriptors of SAM proposals against references built from CAD models, surpassing prior methods by 19.8% AP on BOP's seven core datasets <Cite id="cnos-2023" />.

<Term id="promptable-segmentation">Promptable segmentation</Term> supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. MOKA uses GroundedSAM masks to propose marked candidate points, then prompts a pretrained VLM to select grasp, function and target keypoints, waypoint regions and motion attributes. Calibrated depth lifts the points into the robot frame, and a separate grasp sampler and motion pipeline produce actions; the prompted method trains no robot policy, though the paper separately studies distilling successful trajectories into one <Cite id="moka-2024" />.
edits.after: <Term id="promptable-segmentation">Promptable segmentation</Term> supplies object masks to MOKA and ReKep, two [keypoint interfaces](/manipulation/hierarchical) with different perception stacks. edits.before:
Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects. Learning a new object takes about 20 minutes, including a handful of scenes; optimization runs 3500 steps in about 13 minutes on one 1080 Ti or Titan Xp, and a static-scene scan takes about 70 seconds. The setup uses a calibrated Kuka IIWA LBR, a wrist-mounted Primesense Carmine 1.09 and a Schunk two-finger gripper, and the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information <Cite id="dense-object-nets-2018" />.

Dex-Net 2.0 scores parallel-jaw grasp candidates. It trains on 6.7 million synthetic datapoints from 1500 object models, each pairing a grasp-aligned depth crop with an analytic robust-epsilon quality label. The planner ranks antipodal candidates, checks reachability and table collision, and works on single-view depth of an isolated object on a planar worksurface, assuming rigid objects and known camera intrinsics. Missing depth on thin parts and collisions remain failure modes, and its pile demonstration separates objects before grasping <Cite id="dexnet-2-2017" />.
edits.after: Dense Object Nets learns a descriptor for each RGB pixel, self-supervised by matches from static RGB-D reconstructions, and demonstrates correspondence across viewpoints and moderately deformable configurations. Class-consistent training generalizes across sufficiently similar hats, shoes and mugs, while instance-specific training distinguishes objects; for grasping, the gripper's 6-DoF orientation needs further information <Cite id="dense-object-nets-2018" />.

edits.before: <Term id="pose-estimation">Pose estimation</Term> turns a mask into a rigid body with a position and orientation, and methods divide by what they assume about the object. Instance-level methods train on specific objects. PoseCNN localizes each object's centre, predicts its distance and regresses a rotation quaternion with a loss that handles symmetric objects. It introduced YCB-Video, 21 objects across 92 videos and 133,827 frames <Cite id="posecnn-2018" />. DOPE, trained only on synthetic domain-randomized and photorealistic data, performs competitively with a network trained on real and synthetic data <Cite id="dope-2018" />.

edits.before: The BOP 2024 report moved the frontier. Its best unseen-object method, FreeZeV2.1, is 22% more accurate on BOP-Classic-Core than GenFlow and 4% behind GPose2023, at 24.9 versus 2.7 seconds per image. Co-op takes 0.8 seconds per image and is 13% more accurate than GenFlow. The 2024 edition added model-free tasks onboarded from reference videos, and the report names 2D detection as the main bottleneck for unseen objects <Cite id="bop-2024" />.

edits.before: <Term id="visual-servoing">Visual servoing</Term> uses vision inside the control loop. Hutchinson, Hager and Corke's 1996 tutorial divides such systems into position-based and image-based classes <Cite id="hutchinson-hager-corke-1996" />. Espiau, Chaumette and Rives's 1992 paper applies a task-function framework to image-based control, with a task function designed for regulation that need not be the raw feature difference. Its interaction matrix relates feature rates to the camera's translational and rotational velocity in the camera frame. Convergence depends on task and model conditions, and neglecting target motion can leave a tracking error <Cite id="espiau-1992" />.

edits.before: For a fixed goal and motionless target, Chaumette and Hutchinson's Part I writes $\dot{s} = L_s v_c$, with $v_c$ the camera's six-component spatial velocity. Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) uses image features, and position-based visual servoing (PBVS) uses estimated pose. The IBVS point-feature interaction matrix still uses depth and camera intrinsics, estimated from current depths or depths at the desired pose <br className="lg:hidden" /><Cite id="chaumette-hutchinson-2006" />.

edits.before: Redundant-feature IBVS is locally asymptotically stable when the interaction matrices have full rank and the estimated pseudoinverse times the true matrix meets a positivity condition. Coarse estimates can change the camera path without changing the final pose, while poor ones can make the system unstable. Large displacements can meet local minima or singularities, and PBVS points can leave the field of view. In PBVS, pose-estimation errors affect final accuracy <br className="lg:hidden" /><Cite id="chaumette-hutchinson-2006" />.

edits.before: Part II (2007) covers interaction-matrix estimation, hybrid and partitioned control, optimization, switching, trajectory planning and target tracking. Its switching and planning methods address visibility, occlusions and joint limits, and its joint-space formulations cover eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand systems <br className="lg:hidden" /><Cite id="chaumette-hutchinson-2007" />. Bateux and colleagues fine-tuned a CNN to estimate the relative pose between current and desired images and kept a pose-based control law <Cite id="bateux-2018" />.

edits.before: Learned servoing can also aim the camera. EyeRobot 2.0, from Ken Goldberg (UC Berkeley) and colleagues (October 2026), swivels the two eye viewpoints of a single stereo camera to fixate a 3D point. A gaze-servoing policy and a fixation selector are both trained with RL on real data. Without wrist cameras, a standard policy on passive stereo fell from 52% to 27% real-world success. EyeRobot 2.0 beat passive stereo by 40% in real trials and, when a grasped object hid the wrist views, more than doubled the success of policies that had them, 48% against 22% <Cite id="eyerobot-2-2026" />.

edits.before: Hand-eye accuracy depends on noise and motion range, so Enebuse and colleagues advise considering those conditions when benchmarking or calibrating <Cite id="enebuse-2022" />. A detector can keep stable image coordinates while the robot misses because the camera transform drifted, and a depth model can improve pixel metrics while grasps fail because invalid values cluster on the target material. Each stage is evaluated in its native output before the geometry that consumes it. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) defines the geometric checks, rerun after camera remounts, lens changes, time-source changes and resizing updates. edits.before: End-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) policies absorb the explicit pipeline into weights. Gemini Robotics is a VLA model that controls robots directly, built on an embodied-reasoning model whose capabilities include object detection, pointing, trajectory and grasp prediction, multi-view correspondence and 3D bounding boxes <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. Such a policy needs no detector class or CAD model for a new object. It also has no hand-eye residual to re-solve when it misses a grasp by 8 mm.

edits.before:
Scene representation is the form in which a robot stores what it knows about its surroundings so that planners, controllers and other consumers can query it <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Representations range from point clouds and occupancy grids to signed-distance fields, meshes and neural fields such as radiance fields and Gaussian splats <Cite id="cadena-2016" /><Cite id="neural-fields-survey-2024" />.

## The ladder, and what each rung can answer

Three queries separate the rungs: whether a cell is free for a planner, which way a surface faces for a contact solver, and what the scene looks like from a viewpoint the sensor never occupied. Cadena and colleagues judge representations by storage size, construction cost and usefulness for the task <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

<SceneRepresentationLadder className="my-6" />

An occupancy map can hold an occluded region as explicitly unknown, as OctoMap does for free and unknown space alongside occupied space <Cite id="octomap-2013" />. Learned reconstructors fill such regions instead: CUT3R can infer unseen regions of a scene by probing virtual, unobserved views <Cite id="cut3r-2025" />.

### Point clouds and occupancy grids

A <Term id="point-cloud">point cloud</Term> is an unordered set of 3D points, and PointNet requires invariance to the order in which they arrive <Cite id="pointnet-2017" />. A region without points is either empty or unobserved, and the store cannot say which.

Moravec and Elfes projected wide-angle sonar readings from different sensors and robot positions onto a 2D <Term id="occupancy-grid">occupancy grid</Term>. Each reading marked a probably empty beam interior and an uncertain reflecting point near the measured range, and overlapping readings refined these constraints. Curless and Levoy fuse range images into a cumulative weighted <Term id="signed-distance-field">signed distance function</Term> and recover the surface at its zero crossing, truncating distance ramps and weights near observed points. Its projective TSDF caps visible-space values at the truncation distance $\mu$, leaves non-visible points beyond $\mu$ unmeasured and is exact at the surface, so fusion yields an approximate pseudo-Euclidean distance. Normals come from numerical derivatives near the zero level set, and ray marching finds surfaces by trilinear interpolation <Cite id="kinectfusion-2011" />.

At manipulation scale it reports up to 10x the speed of the state of the art in 8x less memory, with up to 99% collision recall <Cite id="curobo-v2-2026" />. A mesh adds connectivity, giving each face a normal and a renderable surface, but leaves holes where nothing was observed, and filling them invents geometry <Cite id="curless-levoy-1996" />.

NeRF fits a <Term id="neural-radiance-field">neural radiance field</Term> to a static scene from posed RGB photographs, intrinsics and scene bounds. Low texture remains the main failure case, and slow motion can delay inertial initialization <Cite id="orb-slam3-2021" />.

Direct Sparse Odometry skips the detector and optimizes photometric error over sampled pixels jointly with geometry <Cite id="dso-2018" />. Features are robust to brightness change, while a direct method can sample any region with intensity gradient, including near-featureless walls, and gains from calibrating exposure, vignetting and camera response <Cite id="dso-2018" />. Learned systems keep classical machinery: DROID-SLAM iterates camera pose and per-pixel depth through a dense bundle-adjustment layer <Cite id="droid-slam-2021" />. AMB3R-SLAM avoids bundle adjustment, which relies on a static world, and enforces consistency in a hierarchical back end <Cite id="amb3r-slam-2026" />. On one consumer GPU it reconstructs kilometer-scale monocular trajectories over 10,000 frames, and it cuts absolute trajectory error on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70% against the previous state of the art <Cite id="amb3r-slam-2026" />.

Monocular ORB-SLAM validates a <Term id="loop-closure">loop closure</Term> geometrically, then spreads its error with similarity alignment and Essential Graph optimization <Cite id="orb-slam-2015" />. <Term id="place-recognition">Place recognition</Term> asks whether the current image matches a stored place, and motion information can also inform that belief. Viewpoint, illumination and seasonal changes alter one place's appearance, and different places can look alike, which is perceptual aliasing <Cite id="lowry-2016-place-recognition" />. Perceptual aliasing can create false-positive associations that corrupt back-end estimates, while false negatives discard useful measurements. Robust losses and loop-closure validation mitigate outliers, though failures remain that depend on initialization <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. Graduated non-convexity solvers tolerate 70 to 80% outliers, without a guarantee of global optimality <Cite id="gnc-2019" />.

In the back end, Square Root SAM estimates the trajectory and landmark map jointly by MAP inference, which under Gaussian models with known data associations is sparse nonlinear least squares. It solves successive linearized systems by QR or Cholesky, and variable ordering controls fill-in <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. Smoothing suits loop closure because relinearizing the past requires the past to stay in the graph. Cadena and colleagues contrast sparse landmark maps with dense models suited to obstacle avoidance, and cite octrees and voxel hashing as efficient volumetric storage. Two rooms can look identical to a 2D laser yet differ to a camera. Severe illumination changes defeat bag-of-words methods, and active range cameras work in dark, untextured scenes but face range and external-light limits <Cite id="cadena-2016" />.

The iMAP system learns a scene-specific MLP from scratch at room scale from a handheld RGB-D stream. It tracks at 10 Hz and maps at 2 Hz on a desktop CPU and GPU, retaining keyframes for replay <Cite id="imap-2021" />. NICE-SLAM uses hierarchical feature grids with pretrained geometry decoders, reconstructs a multi-room apartment and performs no loop closure <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. Its 47 ms tracking and 130 ms mapping times use small pixel samples on an RTX 3090 <Cite id="nice-slam-2022" />. SplaTAM maps with 3D Gaussians from an RGB-D camera and uses a silhouette mask to determine whether areas were previously mapped <Cite id="splatam-2023" />. Gaussian Splatting SLAM runs monocular SLAM live at 3 fps with Gaussians as the only representation <Cite id="monogs-2023" />. Systems on learned 3D priors report higher frame rates: MASt3R-SLAM runs at 15 FPS with loop closure and second-order global optimization <Cite id="mast3r-slam-2024" />. SLAM3R reconstructs from monocular video at 20+ FPS without solving camera parameters <Cite id="slam3r-2024" />. Navigation2, built on ROS 2, uses a layered costmap. Its global planner computes a shortest route to the goal, and a separate controller computes a local path and control signals, each a plugin in an asynchronous server <Cite id="nav2-2020" />. ## A representation is a service contract

[Perception](/classical/perception) locates objects in the current frame. Consumers issue different queries: localization needs stable landmarks, collision checking needs occupied volume and a conservative update rule, grasping needs surface pose and identity, and rendering needs appearance. Hydra stacks rungs in one real-time system, building a local ESDF, extracting a topological map of places from it and segmenting places into rooms <Cite id="hydra-2022" />. ConceptFusion fuses pixel-aligned open-set features into 3D maps through traditional SLAM <Cite id="conceptfusion-2023" />. ConceptGraphs builds open-vocabulary, graph-structured 3D scene representations because per-point feature maps do not scale well to larger environments <Cite id="conceptgraphs-2023" />.

SceneLM, from Jitendra Malik (UC Berkeley), Marco Pavone and colleagues (September 2026), keeps the whole map as a structured text list of objects that one vision-language model edits after each image. On language-grounded retrieval and localization benchmarks it performed competitively with complete mapping pipelines, with a map 6 to 12 times more compact, and it ran online on an edge device aboard a quadruped <Cite id="scenelm-2026" />.

Ledger, from Shravan Chaudhari, Homanga Bharadhwaj and colleagues at Johns Hopkins (October 2026), keeps a persistent 3D object memory from a person's egocentric video: each object's resting locations, its moves and a short description, retained after it leaves view. A language model answering from these records as text, without the images, raised GPT-5.4's HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, and on Ego4D the memory located objects with a median error of 0.99 m where it returned a prediction <Cite id="ledger-2026" />.

A deployed map publishes its frame, timestamp, resolution, unknown-state convention, update rate and invalidation rule. In MoveIt 2, the planning scene holds the robot's current state, its model and the world representation for collision checking, and a monitor maintains it from parameters and topic subscriptions <Cite id="moveit-planning-scene-2026" />. Attached or removed objects must reach that view before motion; the [ROS 2 guide](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers) covers transforms and the planning scene. A scene representation answers what is present now, while a world model must answer how state changes under an action, as the [simulator comparison](/world-models/world-models-vs-simulators) sets out.

edits.before: State estimation is the computation of a robot's state, such as its [configuration](/classical/kinematics) or velocity over ground, from noisy, biased and intermittent sensor readings. Probabilistic estimators report a belief, so each estimate carries its uncertainty <Cite id="thrun-2005" />. [Planning](/classical/motion-planning) and [control](/classical/control) assume that this state is known.

edits.before: The gain is prior uncertainty over prior-plus-sensor uncertainty. A filter that trusts its model gets a small gain and mostly ignores the sensor; one that trusts its sensor gets a gain near one. Under linear-Gaussian assumptions the recursion is the minimum-variance estimator, and Kalman's projection-based derivation makes it the best linear estimator with white noise even without Gaussian noise <Cite id="kalman-1960-filter" />. Kalman and Bucy's 1961 continuous-time filter derives a Riccati equation for the covariance of the optimal filtering error <Cite id="kalman-bucy-1961" />.

edits.before: Linearization holds near the estimate, which is the uncertain quantity. Where the nonlinearity is strong over the region the covariance covers, $\Sigma$ stops describing the true error, and the filter grows overconfident and can diverge <Cite id="mcgee-schmidt-1985" /><Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. Julier and Uhlmann summarize 35 years of experience: the EKF is difficult to implement and tune, and reliable only for systems almost linear on the time scale of the updates <Cite id="julier-uhlmann-2004" />. Li and Mourikis proved that standard EKF visual-inertial odometry is inconsistent because of how its Jacobians are computed, so it underestimates its uncertainty <Cite id="li-mourikis-2013" />. Smith, Self, and Cheeseman's stochastic map propagated first-order covariance estimates of spatial relationships and required small angular errors, because it linearizes inherently nonlinear relationships <Cite id="smith-1990" />.

The unscented Kalman filter of Julier and Uhlmann keeps the Gaussian and pushes deterministically chosen sample points through the true nonlinearity <Cite id="julier-uhlmann-1997" />. Particle filters drop the Gaussian assumption and carry the belief as a set of particles <Cite id="thrun-2005" />.

edits.before: Dellaert and Kaess's 2006 Square Root SAM jointly estimates the <Term id="slam">SLAM</Term> trajectory and landmark map, assuming known data associations, Gaussian models, a uniform landmark prior and a fixed initial frame. It solves successive linearized systems, by QR on the measurement Jacobian or Cholesky on the information matrix, and variable ordering sets fill-in and cost <Cite id="dellaert-kaess-2006" />. The iSAM method updates only the part of the factorization a new measurement touches <Cite id="kaess-2008" />. iSAM2 adds a Bayes tree with incremental reordering and relinearization: an update re-eliminates the affected cliques and their ancestors, then reattaches unaffected subtrees. Thresholds trade accuracy for computation, and a large loop closure can cost as much as a batch solve <Cite id="kaess-2012" />.

edits.before: Cadena and colleagues describe a classical SLAM period from 1986 to 2004, with EKF, Rao-Blackwellised particle-filter and maximum-likelihood approaches, and an algorithmic-analysis period from 2004 to 2015 <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. In Rao-Blackwellized grid mapping, each particle carries its own map <Cite id="grisetti-gmapping-2007" />. The survey treats MAP estimation, often over factor graphs, as the de facto standard but notes EKF systems with state-of-the-art performance. The gap shrinks when EKF linearization is accurate, sliding windows are used and inconsistency is addressed, and graphs still face unbounded growth and information loss under sparsification <Cite id="cadena-2016" />. The MSCKF sliding-window filter keeps 3D feature positions out of the state and is optimal up to linearization errors <Cite id="msckf-2007" />. OKVIS argues that nonlinear optimization offers superior accuracy while staying tractable through sparsity <Cite id="okvis-2014" />. [Scene representation and mapping](/classical/scene-representation) covers what a robot keeps from the estimate.

Backprop KF optimizes a filter as a deterministic computation graph, so convolutional networks can read raw images <Cite id="backprop-kf-2016" />. TLIO regresses 3D displacement and its uncertainty from IMU data and fuses both into a stochastic cloning EKF <Cite id="tlio-2020" />. AirIO pairs a learned inertial model with an uncertainty-aware EKF for aggressive UAV flight <Cite id="airio-2025" />. MAC-VO learns a metrics-aware keypoint covariance and uses it to weight pose graph optimization <Cite id="mac-vo-2024" />.

edits.before: Fusing visual and inertial measurements requires each measurement's precise sampling time <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />. Samples with the same receipt time can describe different instants, and most consumer cameras use rolling shutters that capture each pixel row at a slightly different time <Cite id="li-rolling-shutter-2013" />. The camera-IMU offset can be a state variable, locally identifiable except in a few degenerate motions <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />. OpenVINS calibrates the camera-to-IMU time offset in its sliding-window filter <Cite id="openvins-2020" />, and Kalibr estimates time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.
edits.after: Fusing visual and inertial measurements requires each measurement's precise sampling time <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />, and most consumer cameras use rolling shutters that capture each pixel row at a slightly different time <Cite id="li-rolling-shutter-2013" />. The camera-IMU offset can be a state variable, locally identifiable except in a few degenerate motions <Cite id="li-mourikis-temporal-2014" />; OpenVINS calibrates it in its sliding-window filter <Cite id="openvins-2020" />, and Kalibr estimates time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.

An action space is the interface between a policy and the rest of the robot: what the network predicts, which errors the controller absorbs, how often inference runs and whether embodiments share labels. In Open X-Embodiment, the same seven numbers can mean absolute or relative positions or velocities <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />. Try the check below.

    {
      value: 'joint-position',

      why: 'The same joint vector places different robots in different physical poses. This is easy to replay on one embodiment and a poor shared task-space label across different kinematic chains.'
    },
    {

    },

    }

## The contract has four parts

A contract names coordinates (joint, Cartesian, object-relative or another frame), semantics (absolute target, delta, velocity, force, torque or controller parameter), timing (rate, horizon and stale-prediction handling) and execution (interpolation, clipping, inverse kinematics, feedback and safety limits). DROID records equivalent commands in several action spaces <Cite id="droid-2024" />, and robosuite's controllers span joint and Cartesian spaces <Cite id="robosuite-2020" />.

## Joint-space actions

Joint position targets are a common imitation baseline: on matched leader-follower rigs, demonstrated angles become labels after calibration checks. ACT uses the leader arms' joint positions as actions, predicting chunks of absolute joint-and-gripper targets for two ViperX arms <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. The controller interpolates, enforces limits and closes a fast loop, but one shoulder angle moves different arms differently.

Joint velocity targets encode increments and can drift when integrated. The [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics/) derives the forward map and Jacobian that both need <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. In locomotion RL, target joint angles with local feedback beat raw torques for learning speed, robustness and motion quality <Cite id="peng-action-space-2016" />.

## Cartesian actions

Cartesian actions say what the tool should do: translate, rotate, open or close. Relative deltas from the current pose can label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike once range and frame are fixed. Each robot then needs inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller, singularity handling and joint-limit avoidance. Khatib's 1987 IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation paper on the operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />.

Euler angles and quaternions are discontinuous as network outputs, while 6D representations are continuous <Cite id="rotation-continuity-2018" />. Axis-angle increments must also name the tool or world frame.

NVIDIA says GR00T N1.7 shares relative end-effector deltas across robot and human embodiments, so priors learned from human video transfer directly to robot control <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. Its N1.6 notes find relative actions smoother and more accurate than absolute ones but prone to error accumulation on small datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />. An action space is the interface between a policy and the rest of the robot: what the network predicts, which errors the controller absorbs, how often inference runs and whether embodiments share labels. In Open X-Embodiment, the same seven numbers can mean absolute or relative positions or velocities <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />.

## The contract has four parts

A contract names coordinates (joint, Cartesian, object-relative or another frame), semantics (absolute target, delta, velocity, force, torque or controller parameter), timing (rate, horizon and stale-prediction handling) and execution (interpolation, clipping, inverse kinematics, feedback and safety limits). DROID records equivalent commands in several action spaces <Cite id="droid-2024" />, and robosuite's controllers span joint and Cartesian spaces <Cite id="robosuite-2020" />.

## Joint-space actions

Joint position targets are a common imitation baseline; ACT predicts chunks of absolute joint-and-gripper targets for two ViperX arms <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. The controller interpolates and enforces limits, but one shoulder angle moves different arms differently.

Joint velocity targets drift when integrated; the [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics/) derives the forward map and Jacobian both need <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. In locomotion RL, target joint angles with local feedback beat raw torques for learning speed, robustness and motion quality <Cite id="peng-action-space-2016" />.

## Cartesian actions

Cartesian actions say what the tool should do. Once range and frame are fixed, relative deltas from the current pose label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike, provided each robot supplies inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller; Khatib's 1987 operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />. Euler angles and quaternions are discontinuous as network outputs, while 6D representations are continuous <Cite id="rotation-continuity-2018" />.

GR00T N1.6's notes find relative actions smoother and more accurate than absolute ones but prone to error accumulation on small datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />, and in matched VLA pretraining ablations a unified end-effector-relative representation was critical for cross-embodiment transfer <Cite id="vla-scaling-alignment-2026" />. X-VLA instead learns a separate set of soft-prompt embeddings for each data source as embodiment-specific prompts <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />.

## Torque and impedance actions

Torque actions expose dynamics and contact; Levine et al. mapped raw images to motor torques <Cite id="levine-visuomotor-2015" />. Impedance actions sit between: the policy picks a pose target plus stiffness and damping, and a controller turns error into force. Hogan judged position or force control alone inadequate for manipulation <Cite id="hogan-1985" />. Task-space impedance references needed the fewest samples against torque, joint PD and inverse dynamics <Cite id="varin-action-spaces-2019" />, and Adaptive Compliance Policy's predicted compliance beats position-only visuomotor policies by over 50% <Cite id="acp-2024" />.

An <Term id="action-chunking">action chunk</Term> predicts several steps per inference, which helped ACT and two retrofitted baselines ([action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking/)) <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />; Diffusion Policy executes the first part of a predicted horizon, then replans <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Open-loop chunks go stale when contact changes the scene, which receding horizons, temporal ensembling and real-time chunk replacement each address <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> ([real-time execution](/manipulation/realtime-execution/)).

Rates differ by layer: GEN-1.5 produces 100 Hz action trajectories <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />, and Helix 02's S0 sends joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz beneath S1's 200 Hz joint targets <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Report predicted and executed horizons separately.

## Tokens change the output geometry

RT-2 <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> and OpenVLA map continuous actions to vocabulary tokens to reuse language-model training, OpenVLA binning seven dimensions into 256 values <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. Binning allows cross-entropy but limits resolution and adds autoregressive decoding to latency. FAST compresses a chunk's frequency coefficients with byte-pair encoding, far better than per-dimension binning, and its universal FAST+ tokenizer was trained on 1M real robot action trajectories <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. VQ-BeT's vector-quantized actions infer 5 times faster than Diffusion Policy <Cite id="vq-bet-2024" />, and LAP writes end-effector motions as short natural-language phrases, with LAP-3B averaging over 50% zero-shot success on three unseen robots <Cite id="lap-2026" />.

Continuous heads skip tokens: OpenVLA-OFT's continuous actions, parallel decoding and L1 objective lifted LIBERO success from 76.5% to 97.1% <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />, and Figure says Helix outputs continuous control to avoid tokenization <Cite id="helix-2025" />. Naively adding a continuous expert to a VLM harms training speed and knowledge transfer, which [knowledge insulation](/manipulation/knowledge-insulation/) addresses <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

Zeji Yi, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon and Amazon FAR (October 2026) gave one PaliGemma VLA four action heads: continuous or binned into 512 values, each predicted in one pass or by iterative flow. On simulated RoboCasa, over five seeds of 500 episodes, binned flow reached 53.9% success, continuous flow 52.7% and one-pass continuous regression 38.8%. One-pass binned prediction reached 27.1%, which the authors trace to tokens chosen independently across time steps and action dimensions; guidance raised it to 49.2% <Cite id="discrete-actions-2026" />.

EgoLAP, from Lihan Zha, Dhruv Shah, Anirudha Majumdar and colleagues at Princeton, Toyota Research Institute and Physical Intelligence (October 2026), trains on human and robot trajectories through a shared chain of language actions that describe motion intent. edits.before: DeepMind's March 2025 report introduces a Gemini 2.0-based family. Gemini Robotics-ER extends spatial and temporal understanding for pointing, trajectory prediction and grasp prediction, and Gemini Robotics builds on ER to produce robot actions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. The March 12, 2025 launch post says Gemini Robotics more than doubles performance on a comprehensive generalization benchmark against other state-of-the-art VLAs, announces an Apptronik humanoid partnership and gives ER to trusted testers <Cite id="gemini-robotics-blog-2025" />.
edits.after: DeepMind's March 2025 report introduces a Gemini 2.0-based family: Gemini Robotics-ER for spatial and temporal understanding, and Gemini Robotics, which builds on ER to produce robot actions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. edits.before: The 1.5 report, first submitted to arXiv on October 2, 2025, interleaves natural-language thinking with VLA actions, introduces Motion Transfer across embodiments and uses the separate GR-ER 1.5 model as an orchestrator. Varying ER's thinking budget shows that the useful amount of thinking depends on the task <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. The launch post, dated September 25, 2025, made ER 1.5 available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini Robotics 1.5 to select partners <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-blog-2025" />.

edits.before:
Gemini Robotics On-Device (June 2025) was the first DeepMind VLA offered for fine-tuning, through an SDK for trusted testers <Cite id="gemini-robotics-on-device-2025" />. ER 1.6, released on April 14, 2026 through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, added reading of gauges and sight glasses, a use case found with Boston Dynamics <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-1-6-2026" />.

On July 30, 2026, DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2 as three models: a VLA that converts vision and language into motor control, the embodied-reasoning VLM ER 2, and On-Device 2 for local operation. Apollo 2 walks, crouches and stretches to manipulate objects, where earlier humanoid models did upper-body tabletop tasks. The SharpaWave hand has 22 <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">DoF</Term>, and the Franka Duo uses two-fingered parallel grippers. One checkpoint runs Apollo 2 with SharpaWave hands, Apollo 2 with Inspire hands and Franka Duo with the Robotiq gripper <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.

ER 2 plans multi-step tasks lasting several minutes, tracks progress, coordinates with the VLA and supports collaboration between robots. DeepMind says On-Device 2 adapts to new bi-arm embodiments in a few hours, typically with fewer than 200 examples, shown on Dexmate, SO101 and Trossen <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. The ER 2 post adds success detection on raw video feeds and instrument reading tested on 10 instrument types <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-2-2026" />.
edits.after: On July 30, 2026, DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2 as three models: a VLA, the embodied-reasoning VLM ER 2, and On-Device 2 for local operation. The ER 2 post adds success detection on raw video feeds <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-2-2026" />.

edits.before: The 1.5 model card specifies continuous numerical actions, plus text when thinking is enabled, but no action-head family, chunk lengths, command rate or parameter count <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. The Gemini Robotics 2 announcement also omits them and Motion Transfer internals. ER 2 launched on Google AI Studio and in private preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the VLA and On-Device 2 went to early-access partners, and weight and licence terms are undisclosed <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. DeepMind validates its Veo-based [world-model](/world-models/) policy simulator against more than 1,600 real trials of eight Gemini Robotics checkpoints <Cite id="veo-world-simulator-2025" />.

edits.before: GR00T N1, first submitted in March 2025, couples a <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> backbone to a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> diffusion-transformer action head that reads vision-language tokens through cross-attention, and links the public GR00T-N1-2B checkpoint <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. N1.6, dated December 15, 2025, doubles the DiT to 32 layers, and NVIDIA reports it outperforms N1.5 in simulation and on real YAM, AgiBot Genie-1 and Unitree G1 robots <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />.

edits.before:
The Isaac-GR00T repository lists N1.7 on April 18, 2026, with a Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone on the Qwen3-VL architecture and a 3B-parameter base checkpoint. The DiT returns from 32 to 16 layers, the state and action interface grows to 132 dimensions, and the prediction horizon to 40. Actions are relative end-effector deltas shared by robot and human embodiments, and pretraining adds 20K hours of EgoScale human video. Inference needs one GPU with 16 GB or more of VRAM <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. The EgoScale paper itself reports over 20,854 hours <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />.

The README's licence section assigns Apache 2.0 to code and the NVIDIA Open Model License to weights, while its introduction calls N1.7 "fully commercially licensable under Apache 2.0". NVIDIA describes N1.7 as comparable to N1.6, with better generalization and language following <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. On March 16, 2026, NVIDIA put N1.7 into early access with commercial licensing and previewed GR00T N2, a DreamZero-based model slated for year-end that it says succeeds at new tasks more than twice as often as leading VLAs <Cite id="nvidia-gtc-gr00t-n2-2026" />.

edits.before: Figure's February 20, 2025 Helix post pairs two systems. S2, an internet-pretrained VLM, produces a continuous latent task representation at 7 to 9 Hz, and S1, a latent-conditioned visuomotor transformer, reads it with images and robot state at 200 Hz. S1 outputs wrist poses, finger flexion and abduction, torso and head orientation targets, and a synthetic task-completion signal. The post calls the S2 backbone open-source and open-weight <Cite id="helix-2025" />.
edits.after: Figure's February 20, 2025 Helix post pairs S2, an internet-pretrained VLM producing a latent task representation at 7 to 9 Hz, with S1, a visuomotor transformer that reads it with images and robot state at 200 Hz and outputs wrist, finger, torso and head targets <Cite id="helix-2025" />.

edits.before: Figure's January 27, 2026 Helix 02 post adds a third layer. S2 interprets scenes and language and sequences latent goals. S1 maps head and palm cameras, fingertip touch and full-body proprioception to full-body joint targets at 200 Hz. S0, a 10M-parameter whole-body controller, outputs joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz. Figure says S0 trains entirely in simulation on over 1,000 hours of joint-level retargeted human motion, using sim-to-real reinforcement learning across more than 200,000 domain-randomized parallel environments. It replaces 109,504 lines of hand-written C++. Its dishwasher demonstration is described as one continuous four-minute task with 61 loco-manipulation actions, implicit error recovery, no resets and no human intervention <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Neither Helix post gives repeated-trial success tables or release terms for the trained policies <Cite id="helix-2025" /> <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.
edits.after: Figure's January 27, 2026 Helix 02 post adds S0, a 10M-parameter whole-body controller that outputs joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz beneath S1's 200 Hz full-body joint targets. Figure says S0 trains entirely in simulation on over 1,000 hours of retargeted human motion and replaces 109,504 lines of hand-written C++, and describes its dishwasher demonstration as one continuous four-minute task with 61 loco-manipulation actions, no resets and no human intervention <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Neither Helix post gives repeated-trial success tables or release terms for the trained policies <Cite id="helix-2025" /> <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

edits.after: Figure's August 25, 2026 Index announcement counts over 16M uploaded videos and commits over \$1B over 12 months to data and compute <Cite id="figure-index-2026" />, and Figure reports that Index pretraining, all else fixed, lifted Helix 2.5's zero-shot success in 30 unseen homes from 9% to 56% <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />.

edits.before: The AgiBot World report, first submitted in March 2025, introduces GO-1 and its vision-language-latent-action (ViLLA) framework. A latent action model learns from consecutive video frames, a VLM-conditioned planner predicts latent action tokens, and an action expert generates low-level actions. Training includes unlabeled human video and cross-embodiment robot data, and the report presents Colosseo as an open platform <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. The repository dates AgiBot World Beta, with 1,003,672 trajectories, to March 1, 2025 and the open-sourcing of GO-1 to September 19, 2025 <Cite id="agibot-world-repo" />.
edits.after: The AgiBot World report (March 2025) introduces GO-1, whose latent action model learns from consecutive video frames, so training can include unlabeled human video alongside cross-embodiment robot data <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. AgiBot presents GO-2 as closing a "Semantic-Actuation Gap": a lower-frequency System 2 generates structured action sequences, a higher-frequency System 1 combines them with live observations, and teacher forcing trains the executor to follow imperfect reasoning. The announcement gives only relative rates for the two modules and says the work was accepted at CVPR 2026 and ACL 2026 <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.

edits.before:
AgiBot presents GO-2 as closing a "Semantic-Actuation Gap" between reasoning and motor commands. Its Action Chain-of-Thought first generates a macro-plan of action intents. A lower-frequency System 2, the "General Commander", generates structured action sequences through Progressive Refinement, and a higher-frequency System 1, the "Agile Executor", combines them with live observations and corrects noise with Residual Refinement. Teacher forcing trains the executor to follow imperfect reasoning. The announcement gives only relative rates for the two modules <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. AgiBot says its action-reasoning work was accepted at CVPR 2026 and its asynchronous architecture at ACL 2026 <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. The ACoT-VLA paper's arXiv record confirms the CVPR acceptance <Cite id="acot-vla-2026" />.

AgiBot reports 98.5% average success across LIBERO Spatial, Object, Goal and Long; 86.6% zero-shot in LIBERO-Plus environments with disturbances; and 82.9% real-world success for a model trained only on simulation, under a Genie Sim 3.0 heading. It claims superiority over π0.5 and GR00T without trial counts, uncertainty, disturbance protocol or comparator versions <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. On LIBERO-Plus, typical VLAs drop from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />.
edits.after: AgiBot reports 98.5% average success across the four LIBERO suites, 86.6% zero-shot in LIBERO-Plus environments with disturbances, and 82.9% real-world success for a model trained only on simulation. It claims superiority over π0.5 and GR00T without trial counts, uncertainty, disturbance protocol or comparator versions <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />, and on LIBERO-Plus typical VLAs drop from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />.

edits.before: Skild AI's January 14, 2026 [Series C](/market-map/) raised \$1.4 billion at a valuation of over \$14 billion. Skild calls its model "omni-bodied" and says it can control robots without prior knowledge of their body form. It names simulation and Internet video for pretraining and teleoperation and deployments for post-training, with teleoperation mapping images and proprioception to joint-torque sequences. Architecture, parameter count, control rate, chunk horizon, benchmark protocol and weight terms are not given <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />.
edits.after: Skild AI's January 14, 2026 [Series C](/market-map/) raised \$1.4 billion at a valuation of over \$14 billion. Skild calls its model "omni-bodied", names simulation and Internet video for pretraining and teleoperation and deployments for post-training, and says the model can control robots without prior knowledge of their body form. Architecture, parameter count, control rate, chunk horizon, benchmark protocol and weight terms are not given <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />.

edits.before: A July 2025 Skild post describes a low-frequency manipulation and navigation policy that feeds a high-frequency low-level policy <Cite id="skild-brain-2025" />, and a September 2025 post describes training on 100,000 simulated robots <Cite id="skild-omni-bodied-2025" />. Skild presents S1 (August 18, 2026) as an in-context learner: shown a video of a task, it executes it. On unseen long-horizon tasks of 4 to 8 minutes, Skild reports 66% cumulative per-step success at 100k hours of pretraining, against 9% for language prompting <Cite id="skild-s1-2026" />. Skild says S1 then learned soccer through 140 years of simulated self-play before transfer to a robot <Cite id="skild-self-play-2026" />. The company also reports passing \$100M in annual recurring revenue with 60+ paying customers <Cite id="skild-arr-2026" />.
edits.after: A September 2025 post describes training on 100,000 simulated robots <Cite id="skild-omni-bodied-2025" />. The company also reports passing \$100M in annual recurring revenue <Cite id="skild-arr-2026" />.

edits.before: Generalist AI says GEN-0 (November 2025) is pretrained on over 270,000 hours of [real-world manipulation data](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck/), growing by 10,000 hours a week, and tested on 6-DoF, 7-DoF and 16+-DoF semi-humanoid robots <Cite id="generalist-gen0-2025" />. It reports that GEN-1 (April 2026), trained from scratch on half a million hours, reaches 99% average success on tasks where earlier models achieve 64%. It also reports GEN-1 works about 3 times faster than the state of the art, with 1 hour of robot data per task <Cite id="generalist-gen1-2026" />. Generalist says GEN-1.5 (August 2026) outputs 100 Hz actions and learns a task from 3 to 12 seconds of one demonstration in context, with 59% average one-shot success across 10 tasks <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />.

edits.before: Simar Kareer and colleagues at Physical Intelligence and Georgia Tech co-fine-tune π0.5 on human data, with 3D hand positions as actions, and relevant robot data, with no special transfer mechanism. Transfer improves with the quantity and diversity of robot pretraining <Cite id="pi-human-to-robot-2025" />. Ruijie Zheng and colleagues' EgoScale adds aligned human-robot mid-training to relative wrist motion and retargeted hand actions, and finds scale and alignment complementary <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. [Cross-embodiment transfer](/manipulation/cross-embodiment/) compares them.
edits.after:
Physical Intelligence and Georgia Tech co-fine-tune π0.5 on human data, with 3D hand positions as actions, and relevant robot data, and transfer improves with the quantity and diversity of robot pretraining <Cite id="pi-human-to-robot-2025" />. EgoScale adds aligned human-robot mid-training and finds scale and alignment complementary <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. [Cross-embodiment transfer](/manipulation/cross-embodiment/) compares them.

Steertuning, from Lerrel Pinto and colleagues at NYU (October 2026), pretrains a 400M-parameter diffusion policy on egocentric human video alone, then adapts it to a new task from 5 human demonstrations with 2 minutes of LoRA fine-tuning and steering toward the closest demonstration. On a mobile manipulator the authors report 71% average success over 12 new tasks, 9 in a rented home and 3 in their lab. On the lab tasks it succeeded in 25 of 30 trials, against 7 with steering alone and none with the short fine-tune alone <Cite id="steertuning-2026" />.

edits.before: LLMs can decompose high-level tasks into mid-level plans zero-shot, but their steps often fail to map to admissible actions <Cite id="huang-zero-shot-planners-2022" />. SayCan (2022) scores each skill in a supplied library twice. The LLM rates its description as the next step, and an <Term id="affordance">affordance</Term> value estimates whether it can succeed in the current state. The product picks the skill to execute, its description is appended to the prompt, and the loop repeats until a termination option wins <Cite id="saycan-2022" />.

edits.before: On the mobile manipulator, picking uses a multitask language-conditioned behavior-cloning policy. The skill library bounds the system, feedback reaches the planner only through the values at the current step, and the paper reports difficulty reacting when a skill fails despite a high value <Cite id="saycan-2022" />.

edits.before: Code as Policies (2022) prompts a code-writing LLM with example instruction-program pairs to generate Python that calls supplied perception and control APIs. Missing functions are generated recursively. Programs can use loops, conditionals, spatial arithmetic and feedback over perception outputs. It assumes feasible instructions and cannot check correctness in advance. Its real robots lift ViLD or MDETR detections to 3D with depth and a pre-registered camera-to-robot transform, and many failures trace to inaccurate detections. Quantitative evaluation covers only a tabletop simulation <Cite id="code-as-policies-2022" />.

edits.before: In September 2026, several groups returned to code-writing planners with coding agents that test and repair their own programs. SimEX, from Jiaheng Hu, Guanya Shi and colleagues, has the agent build a robot toolbox in simulation and then correct the simulator from a few physical trials; the authors report towel folding, barcode scanning and plate manipulation learned with no demonstrations and 10 minutes of real-robot interaction <Cite id="simex-2026" />. EmbodiedSWE, from Zeyu Shen, Dhruv Shah and colleagues, expands one verified coding-agent solution into many simulated demonstrations, and a VLA fine-tuned only on those demonstrations completed a long-horizon task on a real robot <Cite id="embodiedswe-2026" />. RoboHarn-Evo, from Shifeng Bao, Cheng Chi and colleagues, keeps the model weights fixed and stores task-level and action-level knowledge that physical feedback revises; after 80 interaction rollouts, held-out success rose from 48.3% to 75.0% with GPT-5.5 and from 70.0% to 88.3% with GPT-6 <Cite id="roboharn-evo-2026" />. ASENA, from An-Chieh Cheng, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu and colleagues, gives a coding agent navigation tools; with simulator feedback, ten passes over recurring 100-task subsets raised success from 72% to 98% on R2R and from 65% to 89% on RxR <Cite id="asena-2026" />. RPG, posted on October 1, 2026 by Yen-Jen Wang, Pieter Abbeel, Haozhi Qi and colleagues at UC Berkeley and Amazon FAR, also keeps the weights frozen: it practices in simulation and revises a symbolic skill library and its system prompt. On held-out starts of 22 manipulation tasks, success rose from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15, and the frozen system succeeded in all 30 physical trials, ten on each of three tasks <Cite id="rpg-2026" />. ENPIRE (CoRL 2026), from Wenli Xiao, Guanya Shi and colleagues, hands the real-robot loop of reset, rollout, verification and code changes to coding agents; the authors report policies trained to 99% success on tasks such as organizing a pin box <Cite id="enpire-2026" />.
edits.after:
In September 2026, several groups returned to code-writing planners with coding agents that test and repair their own programs. SimEX has the agent build a robot toolbox in simulation and correct the simulator from a few physical trials, and its authors report towel folding, barcode scanning and plate manipulation learned with no demonstrations and 10 minutes of real-robot interaction <Cite id="simex-2026" />. RPG (UC Berkeley and Amazon FAR, October 2026) keeps the weights frozen and revises a symbolic skill library and its system prompt through practice in simulation; on held-out starts of 22 manipulation tasks, success rose from 28.6% to 95.0% after 15 rounds, and the frozen system succeeded in all 30 physical trials <Cite id="rpg-2026" />.

RAX, from Yilun Du, Pieter Abbeel and colleagues at Harvard, UC Berkeley, NVIDIA, MIT and Stanford (October 2026), gives a coding agent no action demonstrations, hand-built action primitives or value functions and keeps its language-model weights fixed; the agent explores online and compiles what worked into control programs. Against the strongest prior learned policy on each of five simulation benchmarks, its mean margin is 37.4 points, from 7.9 on HumanoidArena, where the agent read three teleoperated demonstrations per task and the baselines trained on 100, to 53.4 on RoboDojo. On a real Franka FR3 and a Rainbow RB-Y1 mobile manipulator the agent received only the task text and the robots' tools. Across the paper's experiments, the agents' model calls used more than 100,000 US dollars of API credits <Cite id="rax-2026" />.

CoEvolve, led from Peking University and Renmin University of China (October 2026), has a multimodal model write the coordination code for two humanoids over frozen SONIC controllers; a verifier checks each executed step, and a rejected step is revised from an accepted checkpoint. With two simulated Unitree G1s carrying a freely supported 0.5 kg payload through corridors in MuJoCo, it finished 8 of 15 runs within an 80-transaction budget across three model backbones, while four adapted baselines given the same GPT-5.4-mini backbone, including CaP-Agent0 and ASPIRE, finished none of their five runs. The authors call these comparisons descriptive because runtime and continuation settings differ, and they report persistent limits in motion precision and contact stability <Cite id="coevolve-2026" />.

No full 6-DoF object pose is needed. It also studies in-context examples and distillation into a policy <Cite id="moka-2024" />.

edits.before: <Term id="knowledge-insulation">Knowledge insulation</Term> (KI) is a training recipe that keeps action learning from damaging a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone. Discrete FAST action tokens train the backbone, while a stop-gradient keeps a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert's gradients out of it <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. Turn off "Protect language skills" to remove the stop-gradient.

edits.before:
1. The action expert trains with flow matching, regressing vector fields of fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, and generates continuous action chunks at inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
2. The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term> plus vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST normalizes actions, applies a DCT to each action dimension over time, and scales and rounds the coefficients, the lossy step. Byte-pair encoding then compresses the flattened sequence losslessly <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. Stop-gradient blocks the expert's updates to the backbone. The expert attends to the image, language and state prefix and to itself, never to FAST tokens; the backbone never attends to it. Stop-gradient on the backbone keys and values the expert reads keeps the forward path and cuts the backward one <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after:
1. The action expert trains with flow matching <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" /> and generates continuous action chunks at inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
2. The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term> plus vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST applies a DCT to each action dimension over time, rounds the coefficients (the lossy step) and compresses the sequence with byte-pair encoding <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. Stop-gradient on the backbone keys and values the expert reads keeps the forward path and cuts the backward one. The expert attends to the image, language and state prefix and to itself, never to FAST tokens, and the backbone never attends to it <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

The paper calls the result "a single transformer with two sets of weights (also known as experts)."
