edits.before: Where [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) denoises with a DDPM, π0 trains the expert with conditional flow matching on a straight path. Sample noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, form $A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1 - \tau)\varepsilon$, and regress $v_\theta$ onto $u = A_t - \varepsilon$, drawing $\tau$ from a beta distribution weighted toward the noisy end. Inference integrates from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = 1$ in 10 forward-Euler steps; the image-text-state prefix is KV-cached once, so each step recomputes only the action suffix <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Lipman et al. found optimal-transport paths more efficient than diffusion paths for training and sampling <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />.

edits.before:
FAST normalizes each action dimension, applies a discrete cosine transform along time, scales and rounds the coefficients, and byte-pair-encodes the flattened sequence. Rounding trades fidelity for compression, and BPE compresses the integers losslessly. The universal FAST+ tokenizer is trained on about one million one-second action chunks across embodiments, action spaces and control frequencies <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />, or "1M real robot action sequences" in PI's post <Cite id="pi-fast-blog-2025" />.

Trained on a 10k-hour cross-embodied mixture, π0-FAST matches π0's generalist performance with up to five times fewer GPU hours <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. Inference costs more: about 750 ms per one-second chunk on an NVIDIA 4090, against within 100 ms for diffusion π0, since decoding needs 30 to 60 tokens instead of ten steps <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. The Knowledge Insulation note reports that π0-FAST took twice as long to finish single-embodiment table bussing <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: π0.5 targets open-world generalization <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. It keeps the π0 skeleton and adds hybrid examples that interleave images, language commands, object detections, semantic subtask predictions and low-level actions. At inference it first predicts a language subtask ("pick up the plate") at low frequency, then conditions the action expert on it at high frequency, with no separate planner. In long-horizon mobile manipulation in new homes, removing either cross-embodiment data source significantly hurts home-task scores; removing web data changes them insignificantly and strongly hurts language following and subtask inference <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. edits.before:
The Knowledge Insulation paper studies how a newly initialized continuous expert interferes with pretrained VLM representations; in one example π0, told to bus a spoon, grasps trash instead. It turns the two-stage π0.5 approach into one stage. The expert trains with flow matching for continuous inference, and the backbone trains on discrete FAST tokens, vision-language data and planning data. Expert gradients stop at the backbone keys and values, the expert attends only to the image, language and state prefix, and the backbone does not attend to the expert <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

With a frozen backbone, shirt folding drops to 0%, and FAST tokens adapt the backbone without action-expert gradients. On generalist table bussing, π0 needs 7.5 times as many training steps to match. Vision-language co-training also gives the joint-training baseline good language following without stop-gradient, and KI's language following improves but stays imperfect <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. The openpi π0.5 checkpoints were trained with KI, but the repository supports only the flow-matching head <Cite id="openpi-repo-2024" />, so outside groups reimplement the FAST loss and KI <Cite id="garg-self-demonstrated-control-2026" />.

edits.before: π*0.6 uses Recap to learn from demonstrations, expert teleoperation corrections and autonomous experience: offline-RL pre-training, task-specific demonstration fine-tuning, then rounds of collecting experience and retraining. A language-conditioned distributional value function predicts negative remaining steps for successes and a large negative value for failures, normalized per task. Each action gets a binary improvement indicator from its advantage and a task-dependent threshold, the policy learns from good and bad data, human corrections are forced positive, and evaluation samples with the positive indicator <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. The report places this formulation closest to CFGRL, which links policy improvement to diffusion guidance <Cite id="cfgrl-2025" />, while outside groups find RL on flow-based π0 and π0.5 hard because flow matching makes action log-likelihoods intractable <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />. edits.before: Real-time execution is delivering a policy's actions on the controller's clock while the next inference runs. edits.before: <Term id="temporal-ensembling">Temporal ensembling</Term>, ACT's 2023 method, queries the policy every timestep and averages its predictions for each timestep with weights $w_i=\exp(-mi)$, where $i=0$ is the oldest retained prediction, so positive $m$ favours older ones <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Averaging predictions from different modes need not give a valid action. In RTC's π0.5 real-robot comparison, both variants triggered the robot's protective stop at +100 and +200 ms of injected latency <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.

edits.before: Real-Time Chunking inpaints the next chunk while the current one executes. Guidance weights are 1 on the first $d$ actions, which execute during inference, 0 on the non-overlapping tail, and decay across the rest of the overlap. It works on diffusion and flow policies without retraining <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> <Cite id="pi-real-time-chunking-blog-2025" />. On six π0.5 real-robot tasks with five denoising steps, RTC's aggregate throughput did not degrade at +0, +100 or +200 ms of injected delay, and it lit matches precisely at total delays above 300 ms <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.
edits.after: Real-Time Chunking inpaints the next chunk while the current one executes, fully weighting the first $d$ actions, which execute during inference, and works on diffusion and flow policies without retraining <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> <Cite id="pi-real-time-chunking-blog-2025" />. On six π0.5 real-robot tasks, its aggregate throughput did not degrade at +0, +100 or +200 ms of injected delay, and it lit matches precisely at total delays above 300 ms <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.

[Real-Time EXPO-FT](/manipulation/rl-finetuning/) learns a lightweight edit policy that reacts to the latest observation while a slow VLA proposes chunks. Chronos Policy, from Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark and Shuran Song at Stanford (October 2026), tells a diffusion transformer when each observation was captured and when each action will run, and randomizes both timings in training. On a simulated conveyor pick-and-place with inference delays up to 200 ms, it kept 76.4% success where Diffusion Policy fell to 1.8%, over 450 episodes per method and condition. On three real tasks with 10 or 20 trials per condition, it had the highest task score under every timing condition, against Diffusion Policy with and without RTC <Cite id="chronos-policy-2026" />.

[Real-Time EXPO-FT](/manipulation/rl-finetuning/) learns a lightweight edit policy that reacts to the latest observation while a slow VLA proposes chunks, raising average performance on four dynamic real tasks from 42% to 97% <Cite id="realtime-expo-ft-2026" />. NVIDIA uses test-time and train-time RTC for GR00T N1.6 <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />, and Figure's Helix offsets its two systems' training inputs to match their deployed latency gap <Cite id="helix-2025" />.

edits.before: In September 2026, Fanding Huang, Cheng Chi, Zhi Wang and colleagues reported ChunkTrust, which infers how many actions to execute before replanning from the policy's own outputs while it runs. Over all 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks it raised π0.5's task-averaged success by 6.80 percentage points, and on four real household tasks it raised the mean normalized process score from 50.4% to 57.5% <Cite id="chunktrust-2026" />.

edits.before: <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> runs several epochs of minibatch updates on a clipped surrogate objective <Cite id="ppo-2017" />, which needs the likelihood of each action taken. <Term id="flow-matching">Flow matching</Term> trains by regressing vector fields along fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, so the executed action's log-likelihood is intractable <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />. edits.before: DPPO (Ren et al., 2024) follows DDPO, which posed diffusion denoising as a multi-step decision problem <Cite id="ddpo-2023" />. DPPO embeds denoising inside the environment MDP: each denoising transition has an analytic Gaussian likelihood, and the environment advances and pays reward only after the final step. Environment-discounted advantages are multiplied by a denoising discount that downweights earlier, noisier steps, and the value function depends on the environment state. Only the last selected denoising steps are fine-tuned, with a frozen copy of the network for earlier ones <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.

A simulation-trained One-leg assembly policy transferred zero-shot to a Franka Emika Panda, with no on-robot RL, and succeeded in 16 of 20 trials at 10 Hz <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.

edits.before: ConRFT (Chen et al., 2025) fine-tunes a consistency-policy action head, a sampler distilled from a diffusion policy <Cite id="consistency-policy-2024" />, while freezing the visual encoders and transformer backbone. Its eight-task study uses Octo-small on a 7-DoF Franka at 10 Hz. Offline Cal-ConRFT pairs a consistency-based <Term id="behavior-cloning">behavior cloning</Term> loss and a negative-Q actor loss with a Cal-QL critic, from 20 to 30 demonstrations per task. Online HIL-ConRFT reweights both actor losses and uses a standard temporal-difference critic. Batches sample equally from demonstration and online buffers, and human takeovers enter the demonstration buffer. The training-noise grid has 40 sub-intervals, and the diffusion-policy baseline uses a five-step setting <Cite id="conrft-2025" />.
edits.after: ConRFT reports 96.3% mean <Term id="success-rate">success rate</Term> across eight tasks, 20 trials each, after 15 to 90 minutes of listed online training. ConRFT's headline 144% is a rounded relative gain over offline Cal-ConRFT's 39.4% mean, which the SFT baseline also scores. Online learning curves can include successes produced by human takeovers, and the paper warns of reward-classifier hacking and limited generalization <Cite id="conrft-2025" />. ConRFT says every compared method used interventions, but PA-RL reports fine-tuning OpenVLA autonomously with Cal-QL, from 40% to 70% in 40 real-world minutes <Cite id="pa-rl-2024" />.

edits.after: pi_RL (Chen et al., 2026) fine-tunes flow-based policies with online PPO. Flow-Noise learns Gaussian noise for denoising transitions jointly with the velocity network and uses the joint likelihood of the denoising path in place of the executed action's marginal likelihood. Flow-SDE uses Gaussian transition likelihoods in a two-layer denoising and environment MDP, with one randomly chosen denoising step stochastic and the rest deterministic <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />.

edits.before:
pi_RL (Chen et al., 2026) fine-tunes flow-based policies with online PPO. Flow-Noise learns Gaussian noise for denoising transitions jointly with the velocity network and uses the joint likelihood of the denoising path in place of the executed action's marginal likelihood; the noise network is dropped for deterministic inference. Main experiments use π0 and π0.5. One configuration fine-tunes the full model with supervision, then freezes the VLM and trains a 300M-parameter action expert on eight H100 80GB GPUs. A September 2026 paper from Seungeun Rho, Wontaek Kim, Danfei Xu and Sehoon Ha studies the same limit using preferences alone. Their PrefPI steers pretrained diffusion policies and π0.5 using relative preferences over the policy's own trajectories, aiming at behaviors the initial policy rarely or never produces; on real hardware, 150 preference-labeled trajectories raised object transport height from 10.7 cm to 19.8 cm <Cite id="prefpi-2026" />.

SeeQ, from Saksham Singh, Aviral Kumar and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon (September 2026), steers at test time with a value function. It learns Q-values for the currently active subtask, which shortens the horizon enough for temporal-difference learning on broad, suboptimal data. Dong and Finn's September 2026 blog post says pretrained VLAs give capable demos with no shared post-training recipe behind them: "RL shows incredible promise in training frontier robotics models, but it is not yet a recipe. On four dynamic real tasks with at most 10 minutes of online data, average performance rises from 42% to 97% with no human intervention <Cite id="realtime-expo-ft-2026" />. Start with [kinematics](/classical/kinematics/): know which frame an object pose and an end-effector delta use, whether rotations compose on the left or right, and where joint limits enter. *Modern Robotics* supplies the vocabulary <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />, and Tedrake warns that sloppy kinematic notation "will inevitably lead to confusion and bugs" <Cite id="tedrake-manipulation-2026" />.

Then study [calibration](/classical/calibration/) and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation/): a drifting camera transform or timestamp mismatch can look like a stochastic policy. Kalibr estimates sensor time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.

Before scaling, record ten episodes and replay them: plot timestamp gaps, render actions onto the robot state, and check units and rotation conventions. Past a threshold per environment or object, more demonstrations add little, and diversity matters far more <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />.

GELLO collects demonstrations more reliably than VR controllers or 3D spacemice <Cite id="gello-2023" />, and LeRobot spans the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack/) from motor middleware to dataset streaming <Cite id="lerobot-paper-2026" />.

edits.before: Open-loop loss is a diagnostic. LIBERO-Plus shifts object layout, camera viewpoint, initial state, language, lighting, background and sensor noise <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />. SIMPLER's simulated scores correlate with real performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />, and RoboArena's double-blind pairwise trials rank generalist policies better than centralized evaluation <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />. edits.before: A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. edits.before: RT-2 (2023) brings web knowledge into control <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized as strings into a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>'s token stream. PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites its 256 least frequently used tokens. The backbone, up to 55B parameters, is co-fine-tuned on robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data, which the authors report generalizes better than robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. PaLM-E had already shown positive transfer from joint web-scale language, vision and visual-language training <Cite id="palm-e-2023" />.

edits.before: Two 2024 releases made the recipe reproducible outside Google. Octo ships 27M- and 93M-parameter checkpoints trained on 800k Open X-Embodiment trajectories, with a separate pretrained T5-base (111M) language tokenizer. Observation and task tokens enter a block-wise-masked transformer; learned readout tokens attend to earlier inputs without being attended to, and a lightweight diffusion head maps them to action chunks. Fine-tuning for a new sensor or output can add positional embeddings, a lightweight encoder or a new head while retaining the transformer weights <Cite id="octo-2024" />.

edits.before: A VLA is two decisions. The prior is the visual, language and robot experience in the backbone; the control interface is the action, horizon, frame and measured rate. A large prior can improve instruction following while a poor interface fails at contact: OFT changed both throughput and success without replacing OpenVLA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />. Before choosing a checkpoint, write down the required semantic novelty, available embodiment data, action contract and latency budget. Pick the prior with the [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models/) and the output with the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces/), then compare only models whose contracts match; [generalist policies](/manipulation/generalist-policies/) and [RL fine-tuning](/manipulation/rl-finetuning/) cover the rest.

edits.before: In character animation, DeepMimic adapted standard RL to imitate motion clips, including retargeted ones, for characters including an Atlas robot model <Cite id="deepmimic-2018" />. AMASS unified 15 optical mocap datasets, over 40 hours and 11,000 motions, in one body parameterization <Cite id="amass-2019" />.
edits.after: DeepMimic adapted standard RL to imitate motion clips, including retargeted ones, for animated characters and an Atlas robot model <Cite id="deepmimic-2018" />.

edits.before: PHC tracks motion and recovers from falls for simulated avatars, with no physical robot. Its rotation-based controller imitates 98.9% of 11,313 filtered AMASS training clips, counting a failure when mean joint deviation exceeds 0.5 m. PMCP freezes learned primitives, trains new ones on progressively harder failed clips, adds a recovery primitive and learns a multiplicative composer. The paper shows reset-free avatar control from webcam pose estimates and language-generated motion, and lists highly dynamic clips, noisy real-time estimates and recovery artifacts as limitations <Cite id="phc-2023" />.
edits.after: PHC tracks motion and recovers from falls for simulated avatars, with no physical robot: its controller imitates 98.9% of 11,313 filtered AMASS training clips, and PMCP trains new primitives on progressively harder failed clips <Cite id="phc-2023" />.

edits.before: On the Unitree H1, H2O's privileged motion-filtering imitator is "similar to PHC" and follows PULSE, which distills a universal motion imitator into a latent representation <Cite id="pulse-2023" />. A separate policy learns whole-body tracking from the cleaned retargeted set with domain randomization, then follows human keypoints estimated in real time from an RGB camera. The deployed <Term id="teleoperation">teleoperation</Term> system also uses robot-side motion capture for linear velocity, with a PD controller under the 19-dimensional joint-target policy <Cite id="h2o-2024" />.
edits.after: On the Unitree H1, H2O's privileged motion-filtering imitator is "similar to PHC" and follows PULSE <Cite id="pulse-2023" />. A second policy learns whole-body tracking from the cleaned retargeted set with domain randomization and follows human keypoints estimated from an RGB camera, but the deployed <Term id="teleoperation">teleoperation</Term> system, a joint-target policy over a PD controller, also uses robot-side motion capture for linear velocity <Cite id="h2o-2024" />.

edits.before: OmniH2O uses kinematic motion goals as a shared interface on the H1. A student distilled from a privileged RL teacher tracks head-and-hand position goals from proprioceptive history, with no explicit global-linear-velocity input, though root odometry still maps goals into the robot frame . Language passes through a text-to-motion model, and a vision-language model picks motion primitives from camera images because it is too slow for direct motor control. A visual policy trained on teleoperated demonstrations feeds the tracker motion goals and hand commands, evaluated on four of six recorded tasks at ten runs each. The authors report no safety guarantees for extreme disturbances or out-of-distribution goals .
edits.after: OmniH2O's student, distilled from a privileged RL teacher, tracks head-and-hand goals from proprioceptive history with no explicit global-linear-velocity input, though root odometry still maps goals into the robot frame . A visual policy trained on teleoperated demonstrations can drive the tracker, evaluated on four of six recorded tasks at ten runs each, and the authors report no safety guarantees for extreme disturbances or out-of-distribution goals .

edits.before: HumanPlus estimates the operator's body and hand poses with one RGB camera. Its Humanoid Shadowing Transformer, trained with PPO on retargeted motion in simulation, deploys zero-shot on a customized H1, reading IMU and joint encoders and outputting joint setpoints for PD control. Two head-mounted cameras record the robot's view during shadowing, and supervised <Term id="behavior-cloning">behavior cloning</Term> then trains a Humanoid Imitation Transformer from binocular images and proprioception. Occlusion, fixed retargeting and limited locomotion remain constraints <Cite id="humanplus-2024" />. TWIST retargets mocap clips and trains one whole-body teleoperation controller with RL plus behavior cloning, covering manipulation, legged manipulation and locomotion <Cite id="twist-2025" />.
edits.after: HumanPlus estimates the operator's body and hand poses with one RGB camera, and its Humanoid Shadowing Transformer, trained with PPO on retargeted motion in simulation, runs zero-shot on a customized H1 from IMU and joint encoders. Two head-mounted cameras record the robot's view during shadowing, and supervised <Term id="behavior-cloning">behavior cloning</Term> then trains a Humanoid Imitation Transformer from binocular images and proprioception; occlusion, fixed retargeting and limited locomotion remain constraints <Cite id="humanplus-2024" />.

edits.before: ExBody had the upper body imitate a reference while the legs only followed a commanded velocity . ExBody2 reports that drifting global keypoint targets can accumulate tracking errors, so it tracks local keypoints with separate velocity tracking. It filters references by an initial policy's lower-body tracking error and distills a privileged PPO teacher into a history-based student that walks, squats and dances on Unitree G1. Its generalist and specialist policies trade coverage against precision, and transitions between specialists remain unresolved . ASAP, the delta-action method in the [sim-to-real module](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer), learns a correction model from real G1 rollouts and fine-tunes against the corrected simulator, producing jumps and sports-style motions .
edits.after: ExBody2 tracks local keypoints with separate velocity tracking, because drifting global keypoint targets can accumulate tracking errors. It filters references by an initial policy's lower-body tracking error and distills a privileged PPO teacher into a history-based student that walks, squats and dances on Unitree G1, though transitions between specialists remain unresolved . ASAP, the delta-action method in the [sim-to-real module](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer), fine-tunes against a simulator corrected from real G1 rollouts for jumps and sports-style motions .

edits.before: KungfuBot trains one policy per processed reference motion. Its adaptive rule tightens the tracking reward's error tolerance from a moving average of tracking error, never loosening it, while curricula lower the early-termination threshold and raise regularization. Its quantitative hardware test is ten Tai Chi trials with the G1 root fixed for evaluation <Cite id="kungfubot-2025" />. Its successor KungfuBot2 is one unified controller with an orthogonal mixture-of-experts, stable over minute-long sequences <Cite id="kungfubot2-2025" />. GMT also trains a single tracking controller, re-clipping long motions and resampling by completion and tracking error. A soft mixture-of-experts teacher, whose gating network combines expert actions, is distilled into a student through DAgger. Its baselines and ablations run in simulation, and it neither gets up after falls nor targets slopes and stairs <Cite id="gmt-2025" />. Learned get-up policies lift a real G1 from lying face up or face down <Cite id="humanup-2025" />.
edits.after: KungfuBot trains one policy per processed reference motion and tightens the tracking reward's error tolerance as training proceeds, never loosening it; its quantitative hardware test is ten Tai Chi trials with the G1 root fixed for evaluation <Cite id="kungfubot-2025" />. GMT instead trains a single tracking controller, distilled from a soft mixture-of-experts teacher whose gating network combines expert actions; its baselines and ablations run in simulation, and it neither gets up after falls nor targets slopes and stairs <Cite id="gmt-2025" />. Learned get-up policies lift a real G1 from lying face up or face down <Cite id="humanup-2025" />.

edits.before: BeyondMimic learns cartwheels, spin-kicks, flip-kicks and sprinting with one setup and shared hyperparameters, composes them through guided latent diffusion and transfers zero-shot to hardware <Cite id="beyondmimic-2025" />. The 2026 robustness work aggregates noisy, inconsistent references with a multi-head cross-attention command encoder and adds a fall-recovery curriculum <Cite id="robust-tracking-2026" />. ZEST trains motion-imitation policies with RL from motion capture, monocular video and animation, and deploys them zero-shot on Atlas, the Unitree G1 and Spot without contact labels or state estimators <Cite id="zest-2026" />. ResGAC, from Guanya Shi (Carnegie Mellon), Koushil Sreenath and colleagues (October 2026), adds residual RL to geometric admittance control on a real Unitree G1 and reports 90% success on a standing peg-in-hole task, against 50% for SONIC <Cite id="resgac-2026" />.
edits.after: BeyondMimic learns cartwheels, spin-kicks, flip-kicks and sprinting with one setup and shared hyperparameters and transfers zero-shot to hardware <Cite id="beyondmimic-2025" />. ZEST trains motion-imitation policies with RL from motion capture, monocular video and animation, and deploys them zero-shot on Atlas, the Unitree G1 and Spot <Cite id="zest-2026" />.

edits.before: Hwangbo and colleagues learned an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators. It predicts joint torque from current and past joint-position errors and velocities, trained on data from exciting the real legs and disturbing the robot by hand. It stands in for actuation in the simulator. Policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models failed to take a single step without falling. A separate recovery policy flipped ANYmal upright from nine tested configurations, including a nearly upside-down pose and two resting on its own legs, after the authors relaxed joint-velocity constraints following the first hardware attempt <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />.
edits.after: Hwangbo and colleagues replaced simulated actuation with a learned network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators, which predicts joint torque from current and past joint-position errors and velocities; policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models failed to take a single step without falling. A separate recovery policy flipped ANYmal upright from nine tested configurations, after the authors relaxed joint-velocity constraints following the first hardware attempt <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />.

edits.before: Lee and colleagues trained a privileged RL teacher to supervise the actions and latent features of a temporal convolutional student. The deployed student reads two seconds of <Term id="proprioception">proprioceptive</Term> history from joint encoders and an IMU, plus the command and current state, with no terrain map. Trained on rigid procedural terrain, ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C controllers crossed mud, snow, rubble and vegetation without environment-specific tuning. The authors warn that a robot commanded off a cliff will walk off it <Cite id="lee-2020" />. RMA, a base policy plus an adaptation module, deployed on the A1 robot without any fine-tuning <Cite id="rma-2021" />; the [sim-to-real module](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer) covers the distillation mechanics.

edits.before: Miki and colleagues fed elevation-map height samples and proprioception to a GRU belief encoder whose learned attention gate controls how much exteroception enters. The student imitates a privileged teacher and reconstructs terrain from noisy observations. With covered sensors on stairs and slippery platforms it fell back on proprioception and revised its terrain estimate after contact. ANYmal C used two Robosense Bpearl LiDARs or four RealSense D435 cameras, with mapping at 20 Hz and the policy at 50 Hz. The Etzel hike covered 2.2 km and 120 m of climb in 78 minutes against a planner's 76, with no falls but stops to reattach a shoe and swap batteries. The authors list possible falls at occluded cliffs or stepping stones <Cite id="miki-2022" />.
edits.after: Miki and colleagues fed elevation-map height samples and proprioception to a GRU belief encoder whose learned attention gate controls how much exteroception enters; the student imitates a privileged teacher and falls back on proprioception when sensors mislead. edits.before: Rudin and colleagues trained flat-terrain walking in under four minutes on one workstation GPU. Their deployment policy used 4,096 ANYmal robots, batches of 98,304 transitions (24 steps per robot) and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU. Their game-inspired terrain curriculum promotes robots that cross a tile, demotes those covering under half the commanded distance, and loops hardest-level solvers back to a random level . The released `legged_gym` repository (October 2021) is the Isaac Gym environment used to train ANYmal on rough terrain .

edits.before: A gait is a footfall-timing pattern: each leg's phase offset in the stride and its duty factor $\beta$, the fraction of the cycle on the ground. Walk These Ways commands a gait as three timing offsets between foot pairs plus a stepping frequency: (0.5, 0, 0) trots, (0, 0.5, 0) bounds and (0, 0, 0) pronks <Cite id="walk-these-ways-2022" />. Alexander linked dynamically similar movement in mammals of different sizes to equal Froude numbers $u^2/gh$ <Cite id="alexander-1984" />.
edits.after:
A gait is a footfall-timing pattern: each leg's phase offset in the stride and its duty factor $\beta$, the fraction of the cycle on the ground. Walk These Ways commands a gait as three timing offsets between foot pairs plus a stepping frequency: (0.5, 0, 0) trots, (0, 0.5, 0) bounds and (0, 0, 0) pronks <Cite id="walk-these-ways-2022" />.

In the MIT Cheetah 2 design, Park, Wensing and Kim plan stance time from stride length and speed, $T_{st} = L/v_d$, keep swing duration fixed, and modulate duty cycle by vertical impulse scaling. Stride length grows with speed only up to 3 m/s, so this is one controller's schedule. Roll instability ended the 6.4 m/s top-speed treadmill run, and at the highest speeds the robot partly leaned on the side wall. edits.before: <Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline RL</Term> learns from a static set of transitions `(observation, action, reward, next observation, termination)` produced by one or more behavior policies <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. For robots, support also spans commanded frame, controller mode, action magnitude, contact regime, task stage and recovery. For robots, support also spans controller mode, action magnitude, contact regime and task stage, and Real-ORL, built on over 6,500 trajectories from 800 robot hours, found that offline RL and imitation prefer different action spaces <Cite id="real-orl-2022" />.

edits.before: Rudin and colleagues define a weighted sum of nine reward terms, including feet air time; the reward is gait-independent, prescribing no gait schedule <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. The initial `legged_gym` commit (October 2021) declares fifteen entries in `LeggedRobotCfg.rewards.scales`. Nine are nonzero: linear- and angular-velocity tracking, vertical linear velocity, roll/pitch angular velocity, joint torque, joint acceleration, feet air time, collisions and action rate. `_prepare_reward_function` drops zero scales and multiplies the rest by the time step. The joint-limit and contact-force functions among its nineteen reward functions are inactive in this config, and the zero-valued `feet_stumble` entry does not match the `_reward_stumble` function, which penalizes feet hitting vertical surfaces. The air-time term rewards long steps on first contact when the planar command norm exceeds 0.1 <Cite id="legged-gym-repo-2021" />.

BVER, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (October 2026), borrows from [bidirectional RRT](/classical/motion-planning/): it grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the start, steering them toward each other. On quadruped box climbing it reached 95% success on a 0.4 m box in about 65% fewer iterations than the best reference-free curriculum it was compared with. It was also the only one of them to learn a 0.7 m box <Cite id="bver-2026" />. Model-based control can also drive the curriculum: ZEST adds a model-based assistive wrench as an automatic curriculum during RL training <Cite id="zest-2026" />.

edits.before: Zhang and colleagues' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller was first posted in 2025 and revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026. It runs on Unitree Go1 and Go2, a Go1 walking on its hind legs into a handstand, and an H1 humanoid tracking a trotting gait. It uses finite-difference derivatives and one warm-started iLQR update per solve, sending joint-angle targets to PD control that the planning model includes. On a 20-core 13th-generation Intel i9, iLQR and TV-LQR feedback run at about 50 Hz and 300 Hz, with a default 0.35 s horizon discretized at 100 Hz. The experiments fuse 100 Hz OptiTrack measurements with 500 Hz joint data, and onboard-only deployment is untested. Raising MuJoCo's impratio from 1 to 100 to reduce slipping doubled a quadruped iteration from 10 to 20 ms <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.

edits.before: <Term id="sample-efficiency">Sample efficiency</Term> is the axis these results turn on. Haarnoja and colleagues learned Minitaur locomotion from 160,000 control steps, about 400 rollouts, in about two hours of real-world time that includes resets and the operator <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. Smith and colleagues learned quadruped walking with model-free RL in 20 minutes in the real world <Cite id="walk-in-the-park-2022" />. DayDreamer trained a Unitree A1 to roll over, stand and walk in one hour without a simulator, and ten more minutes of online learning under pushes produced resistance to light pushes or recovery from harder ones. The authors intervened manually at the edge of the training area without changing the robot's joint configuration or orientation <Cite id="daydreamer-2022" />. In 2026, an online model-based RL controller learned directly on an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator, without demonstrations or simulation pretraining. After 20 minutes of interaction its tracking accuracy was comparable to that of earlier learned controllers trained on 100 to 150 minutes of data <Cite id="excavator-mbrl-2026" />.

edits.before:
<Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline reinforcement learning</Term> learns a policy from a fixed dataset of transitions without further environment interaction during training, then deploys it <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. It can reuse corpora like those in the [datasets module](/data-hardware/datasets). Levine, Kumar, Tucker and Fu identify distributional shift as a central challenge. A learned policy can choose actions outside the behavior distribution, Bellman targets then use erroneously high Q-values for them, and later backups propagate the errors without fresh feedback. The tutorial assumes the data covers enough high-reward transitions for learning to be feasible <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. BCQ showed that extrapolation error leaves standard off-policy algorithms such as DQN and DDPG unable to learn from fixed batches uncorrelated with the current policy <Cite id="bcq-2018" />.

Conservative value estimation pushes estimates down where data is thin: CQL learns a lower bound on policy value by penalizing Q-values on out-of-distribution actions and raising them under the data distribution <Cite id="cql-2020" />. IQL avoids the query entirely, fitting an expectile over dataset actions so the state value acts as an implicit maximum, then extracting the policy by advantage-weighted regression <Cite id="iql-2022" />. TD3+BC adds a behavior-cloning term and state normalization to an off-policy actor-critic and matches far more elaborate offline methods <Cite id="td3-bc-2021" />.

Q-Transformer discretizes each action dimension and backs up Q-values autoregressively with a Transformer conditioned on observation history and earlier action dimensions. It adds conservative regularization and Monte Carlo and n-step returns, and its real-robot experiments mix successful human demonstrations with failed autonomous trials under sparse success rewards, and online fine-tuning is left for future work <Cite id="q-transformer-2023" />.
edits.after: <Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline reinforcement learning</Term> learns a policy from a fixed dataset of transitions without further environment interaction during training, then deploys it <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. BCQ showed that this extrapolation error leaves standard off-policy algorithms unable to learn from fixed batches <Cite id="bcq-2018" />, and CQL answers it by learning a lower bound on policy value, penalizing Q-values on out-of-distribution actions <Cite id="cql-2020" />.

edits.before: Mandlekar and colleagues found batch RL weak on human demonstration data. BCQ did well on suboptimal, multimodal agent-generated data, but neither BCQ nor CQL did well on human datasets, a result the authors say "puts the ability of such algorithms to learn from more natural dataset distributions into question". History-dependent BC-RNN was a strong baseline, and the authors note that human demonstrators can act on more than the current observation <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />.
edits.after: Mandlekar and colleagues found batch RL weak on human demonstrations: neither BCQ nor CQL did well on human datasets, while history-dependent BC-RNN was a strong baseline <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />. Kumar, Hong, Singh and Levine give sufficient conditions under which offline RL beats BC, assuming coverage of the optimal policy; with noisy data that improves coverage, conservative offline RL has a better bound than BC on equal expert data, while on expert data similar performance is a worst-case result. Their drawer-manipulation comparison, in simulation, pits BC on expert successes against CQL on noisy scripted data. Naive CQL can perform no better than BC <Cite id="offline-rl-vs-bc-2022" />.

edits.before:
Kumar, Hong, Singh and Levine give sufficient conditions under which particular offline RL algorithms beat BC. Their theory assumes coverage of the optimal policy and horizon-independent trajectory returns, and they test tabular algorithms on gridworlds and CQL against BC on simulated manipulation, navigation and Atari. With noisy data that improves coverage, conservative offline RL has a better horizon-dependent bound than BC on equal expert data, while on expert data similar performance is a worst-case result. Their drawer-manipulation comparison, in simulation, pits BC on expert successes against CQL on equally sized noisy scripted data. Naive CQL can perform no better than BC <Cite id="offline-rl-vs-bc-2022" />. For teleoperation data, a supervised [behavior-cloning baseline](/manipulation/bc-foundations) is the simpler starting point.

Newer real-robot results favor RL. Offline RL pretrained on diverse robot data learned new tasks in a new domain on a real WidowX from as few as 10 demonstrations <Cite id="ptr-2022" />. Generalist policies fine-tuned on RL-generated data beat the same policies trained on human demonstrations by up to 40% in success <Cite id="rldg-2024" />. Physical Intelligence's RECAP pretrains a VLA with offline RL and more than doubles task throughput on some of the hardest tasks <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. RL-100 reports 1000 of 1000 successful real-robot episodes <Cite id="rl-100-2025" />.

Offline data can also seed online learning. RLPD starts online off-policy training from a buffer already holding offline data, with no pretraining phase or explicit conservatism <Cite id="rlpd-2023" />, and HIL-SERL builds on RLPD with human demonstrations and online corrections <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />. Cal-QL changes one line of CQL so that offline initializations fine-tune well online, beating prior methods on 9 of 11 benchmarks <Cite id="cal-ql-2023" />. Q2RL extracts a Q-function from a behavior-cloning policy and switches between cloned and RL actions by their Q-values; on a real robot it learned pipe assembly and kitting in one to two hours of online interaction <Cite id="q2rl-2026" />.
edits.after: For teleoperation data, a supervised [behavior-cloning baseline](/manipulation/bc-foundations) is the simpler starting point, though newer real-robot results favor RL. edits.before: A robot that has never completed a task has no successful trajectory, and a completion-only reward gives its value function nothing to fit. Shaping is one answer ([reward design](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc)). <Term id="hindsight-experience-replay">Hindsight experience replay</Term> targets sparse binary rewards directly, storing transitions under their original goal and alternative goals and recomputing the reward for each. Its simplest strategy uses the goal achieved in the final state, and its future strategy samples goals achieved later in the same episode <Cite id="her-2017" />.

edits.before: Andrychowicz and colleagues trained DDPG with HER on a simulated seven-DoF Fetch arm for pushing, sliding and pick-and-place, and the future variant learned all three where DDPG alone did not. Pushing added a contact-penetration penalty, and pick-and-place started half its training episodes with the box already grasped. A simulation-trained pick-and-place policy transferred to a physical Fetch without real-robot fine-tuning, using a separately trained camera estimator. HER needs an achieved-goal mapping and a reward recomputable for any replacement goal, and training on multiple goals can help even when only one matters at deployment <Cite id="her-2017" />.

edits.before: A simulated episode restarts from a fresh state for free. A physical episode ends wherever the robot is, and a person or a learned behavior has to put it back. Zhu and colleagues name three requirements for real-world RL: learning from raw sensory inputs, assigning rewards without hand-designed perception or instrumentation, and learning without human episode resets. A D'Claw hand learned valve rotation and bead manipulation from RGB images after people supplied goal examples; training ran unattended, but evaluation included manual resets for bead manipulation. The authors leave sample complexity, exploration on harder tasks and safe operation to future work <Cite id="real-world-rl-ingredients-2020" />.
edits.after: A simulated episode restarts from a fresh state for free; a physical one ends wherever the robot is, and a person or a learned behavior has to put it back.

edits.before: Leave No Trace learns a reset policy alongside the forward policy and uses its value function to abort before non-reversible states, reducing manual resets <Cite id="leave-no-trace-2017" />. Sharma and colleagues' EARL benchmark separates deployed-policy evaluation, which sums gaps to optimal deployment return over training, from continuing-policy evaluation, the limiting average reward of the agent's own actions, and treats interventions as constrained costs. Its experiments still schedule resets during training and stop after a fixed step budget, and the authors note that the two objectives can favor different behavior <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />. VaPRL, from the same group, cuts required interventions by three orders of magnitude against episodic RL on simulated robotics tasks <Cite id="vaprl-2021" />.

Leave No Trace learns a reset policy alongside the forward policy and aborts before non-reversible states <Cite id="leave-no-trace-2017" />. Sharma and colleagues' EARL benchmark sums gaps to optimal deployment return over training and treats interventions as constrained costs, though its experiments still schedule resets during training <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />.

edits.before: <Term id="reset-free-learning">Reset-free learning</Term> replaces manual resets with learned recovery behaviors. Gupta and colleagues' MTRF sequences task-specific policies with a designer-provided task graph, so re-centering, pickup and flip-up restore the conditions for in-hand reorientation after a drop. A D'Hand on a Sawyer arm learned valve reorientation and pipe insertion without manual episode resets. The setup still used supplied rewards, motion capture for the in-hand object, scripted arm motion for pickup, and a user who positioned the objects and started the robot. Pipe insertion used frozen fingers and separate approach and insertion tasks to reduce collisions, and the method assumes that successful upstream tasks leave valid starting states for downstream ones <Cite id="reset-free-rl-2021" />. Without such a task graph a person handles the reset, a cost the human-in-the-loop line pays deliberately <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />.

edits.before: Sim-to-real transfer is getting a policy trained in simulation to work on the physical robot. Its four method families are <Term id="domain-randomization">domain randomization</Term>, <Term id="teacher-student-distillation">teacher-student distillation</Term>, <Term id="system-identification">system identification</Term> and real-to-sim reconstruction. Aljalbout and colleagues' survey covers all four, splitting methods that reduce the gap from those that overcome it <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />.

edits.before: Jakobi and colleagues found in 1995 that sim-to-real correspondence depended on how much noise the simulation used, with very good results at realistic levels <Cite id="jakobi-1995" />. Tobin and colleagues randomized textures, lighting and camera pose for tabletop object localization. After a small hyperparameter search, their best network localized objects to about 1.5 cm, a summary over 480 webcam images of eight geometric objects in object-only, distractor and partial-occlusion conditions. Most runs used ImageNet initialization, though random initialization nearly matched it given enough simulated data, and a Fetch robot used the detector with a motion planner. Their abstract frames the real world as "just another variation" once the simulator varies enough <Cite id="tobin-2017" />.

edits.before: RoboRender, from Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei (Stanford) and colleagues (October 2026), turns simulated trajectories into photorealistic videos for policy training; its policies average 71% real-world success across pick-and-place, articulated-object and mobile manipulation, about 7.1 times raw simulation renderings and 3.6 times conventional visual domain randomization <Cite id="roborender-2026" />.

A recurrent policy trained only in simulation pushed a puck with a seven-DoF Fetch arm, with start and target positions randomized within a 30 cm square <Cite id="peng-2018" />.

edits.before: Peng and colleagues randomized link mass, joint damping, puck mass, friction and damping, table height, controller gains, action timing and observation noise, maximizing expected return over [that dynamics distribution](/how-robots-work/#worlds). A recurrent policy trained only in simulation pushed a puck with a seven-DoF Fetch arm. Real trials used motion capture, 200 control steps per episode, start and target positions randomized within a 30 cm square, and success within 7 cm at the end. The authors report substantial joint-trajectory mismatch after limited calibration and ablate their randomization choices <Cite id="peng-2018" />.
edits.after: OpenAI's 2018 hand policy randomized friction coefficients and object appearance and transferred to the physical robot <Cite id="openai-dactyl-2018" />. Isaac Lab, the [GPU-parallel training framework](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl), ships ADR as a configurable curriculum with reference configs in its dexterous-manipulation examples. In Isaac Lab, simulation state is GPU-resident, but mass, friction, contact offsets and joint armature change through PhysX CPU APIs. Most parameters randomize at runtime, mesh scale and collider type only before simulation starts, and CPU parameter writes can occur beyond episode resets <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />.

SPI-Active notes that poorly tuned randomization "can lead to overly conservative policies" <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />, and Chen and colleagues bound the gap between a randomized policy and the real-world optimum, stressing history-dependent policies <Cite id="chen-dr-theory-2021" />. edits.before: Lee and colleagues distilled a privileged RL teacher, which saw simulator-only terrain and contact information, into a temporal convolutional student via its actions and latent features. The student uses two seconds of <Term id="proprioception">proprioceptive</Term> history from joint encoders and an IMU, plus the command and current state, with no terrain map. Trained on rigid procedural terrain, one controller per robot generation took ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C robots through mud, snow, rubble and vegetation without environment-specific tuning <Cite id="lee-2020" />.

Isaac Lab's DextrAH-RGB example distills a privileged KUKA and Allegro teacher into a stereo-RGB network <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />, and VIRAL's authors report that scaling to tens of GPUs, up to 64, made teacher and student training reliable for an RGB humanoid that ran up to 54 loco-manipulation cycles <Cite id="viral-2025" />.

Agarwal and colleagues distilled a teacher trained on a cheap depth variant into a depth-camera student <Cite id="agarwal-vision-2022" />, and Isaac Lab's DextrAH-RGB example distills a privileged KUKA and Allegro teacher into a stereo-RGB network <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. VIRAL's authors report that scaling to tens of GPUs, up to 64, made teacher and student training reliable, and their RGB humanoid ran up to 54 loco-manipulation cycles <Cite id="viral-2025" />.

RebarSim, from Abhishek Gupta (University of Washington) and colleagues (September 2026), distills an RL teacher trained over procedurally generated rebar into a student that sees multi-view RGB and proprioception. The student seated real factory rebars at 1.4 mm clearance in 91.3% of zero-shot rollouts, and removing appearance randomization or the DAgger mixture sharply lowered success <Cite id="rebarsim-2026" />.

RMA trains a base policy and an environment-factor encoder jointly with RL, then regresses an adaptation module on simulated state-action histories to predict the latent extrinsics. At deployment the base policy maps current state, previous action and estimated extrinsics to desired joint positions. The module reads 50 state-action steps (0.5 seconds) and updates asynchronously at about 10 Hz on the A1, while the base policy runs at 100 Hz on the latest estimate, with no online gradient updates. The paper reports adaptation in fractions of a second without real-world fine-tuning, and failures after large perturbations or multiple leg obstructions. Its latent encodes behavior-relevant conditions without guaranteeing each physical parameter <Cite id="rma-2021" />. UP-OSI had earlier fed dynamics parameters predicted from recent history into a universal policy <Cite id="up-osi-2017" />.

edits.before: Randomization averages over model error, and system identification measures it. Hwangbo and colleagues fitted an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators to real excitation data and used it in simulation to train policies. It predicts torque from joint-position errors and velocities now and 0.01 and 0.02 seconds earlier. Policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models failed to take a single step without falling <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. Tan and colleagues paired an identified actuator model and simulated latency with randomization, perturbations and a compact observation space <Cite id="tan-quadruped-2018" />.

edits.before: Newer methods identify parameters directly. SPI-Active samples them in parallel with Fisher-information-driven excitation and beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion tasks <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />. Miller and colleagues score Spot simulation against hardware with Wasserstein distance and maximum mean discrepancy and tune it with CMA-ES <Cite id="miller-spot-2025" />. HALO calibrates a humanoid and then its payload in differentiable MuJoCo XLA <Cite id="halo-payload-2026" />. ZEST selects joint gains from approximate analytical armature values for closed-chain actuators and adds a refined actuator model; its policies, trained entirely in simulation, deploy zero-shot on Atlas, the Unitree G1 and Spot <Cite id="zest-2026" />.
edits.after: ASAP pretrains phase-conditioned tracking policies in IsaacGym on <Term id="retargeting">retargeted</Term> human motions, runs them on a Unitree G1, and records trajectories with motion capture and onboard sensors. A second PPO policy learns a delta action added before the simulator step, the tracking policy is fine-tuned with the frozen delta model in simulation, and only the tracking policy is deployed. For the hardware study the delta covers only four ankle DoFs of the 23-DoF model <Cite id="asap-2025" />.

edits.before:
Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues apply identification to the objects a robot handles in ForceTwin (September 2026). A person probes a door or another articulated object with a handheld force-sensing gripper, and the system fits inertia, friction, damping and a neural residual for configuration-dependent forces such as door closers. It nearly halves the inertial-parameter error of a vision-language-model prior, and whole-body door-traversal policies trained in its twins were deployed on real robots <Cite id="forcetwin-2026" />.

ASAP pretrains phase-conditioned tracking policies in IsaacGym on <Term id="retargeting">retargeted</Term> human motions, runs them on a Unitree G1, and records trajectories with motion capture and onboard sensors. A second PPO policy maps simulated state and recorded action to a delta action added before the simulator step, rewarded for matching the recorded real trajectory, so no residual labels are needed. The tracking policy is fine-tuned with the frozen delta model in simulation, and only the tracking policy is deployed. For the hardware study the delta covers only four ankle DoFs of the 23-DoF model <Cite id="asap-2025" />.

Evaluation separates IsaacGym-to-IsaacSim and IsaacGym-to-Genesis tests, with open-loop replay and closed-loop tracking over 43 motion sequences grouped by difficulty, from the G1 study. SysID and delta dynamics are simulation baselines, and ASAP does not win every metric: in the easy IsaacSim closed-loop group its mean global joint-position error is 106 mm against SysID's 105 mm. On hardware, compared only with Vanilla, the error falls from 61.2 to 50.2 mm on kicking and from 159 to 112 mm on LeBron James's "Silencer". Pretraining uses basic domain randomization, and the random-action-noise ablation is a Genesis test <Cite id="asap-2025" />.

ASAP reports better tracking on the held-out "Silencer" motion and better out-of-distribution replay with more data, without establishing coverage of arbitrary unseen skills. Its stated hardware limits are motor overheating and damage, motion-capture dependence and the data needed for a full 23-DoF delta model <Cite id="asap-2025" />. Swift's champion-level drone racing likewise combined simulation RL with physical-world data <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

RialTo builds digital twins from small amounts of real data and runs RL in them, raising imitation-policy robustness by over 67% <Cite id="rialto-2024" />. Zhang and colleagues build soft-body splat twins from video whose rollouts correlate strongly with real execution <Cite id="softbody-splat-eval-2025" />. PolaRiS turns short video scans into interactive environments that track real generalist-policy performance better than existing benchmarks <Cite id="polaris-2025" />. SimFoundry builds sim-ready twins from a video and edits them into digital cousins; across 7 tasks and 5 policy architectures its simulated evaluations correlated with real results at a mean Pearson coefficient of 0.911 <Cite id="simfoundry-2026" />. GRAIL generates humanoid interaction data from 3D assets and video-model priors, and visual policies trained only on it reached 84% success on object pick-up and 90% on stair-climbing on a real Unitree G1 <Cite id="grail-2026" />. Kaiyuan Chen, Ken Goldberg and colleagues at UC Berkeley and NVIDIA (October 2026) built RoboSimStudio, which lets people and coding agents edit the solver, contact model and physical parameters of a Newton simulation <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />. In a pilot, coding agents built a bimanual sponge-wiping simulation from a smartphone video in about an hour, and a policy improved there completed the wipe on the real robot <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />. One real rollout then displaced a bar support that the simulation held fixed, and the authors judged sim and real agreement on this single task mainly by qualitative observation <Cite id="robosimstudio-2026" />.

edits.before: The survey also covers co-training with real-world data, noting its benefit for robotic foundation models such as GR00T N1. It says the action space "plays a crucial role in reducing the sim-to-real gap" across navigation, locomotion and manipulation, citing joint-velocity control for manipulation, and that high-frequency impedance controllers can improve manipulation transfer <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Co-training has since become a headline recipe. Maddukuri and colleagues report that simulation data raises real-world performance by 38% on average <Cite id="sim-real-cotraining-2025" />, and Lei and colleagues identify structured representation alignment as its primary effect <Cite id="lei-cotraining-2026" />.

Haarnoja and colleagues' soccer humanoid transferred through high-frequency control, targeted dynamics randomization and training perturbations <Cite id="haarnoja-soccer-2023" />. Actuator reality shaping makes physical actuators match the simulator's idealized dynamics <Cite id="actuator-reality-shaping-2026" />, and Boston Dynamics reports fewer fidelity issues because Atlas's model and hardware are extremely close <Cite id="bd-atlas-hard-work-2026" />.

edits.before: The locomotion and manipulation asymmetry is the pattern in which simulation-trained reinforcement learning (RL) made legged locomotion robust well before general manipulation. In 2021 an ANYmal quadruped learned to walk on flat ground in under four minutes, and on uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.
edits.after: Simulation-trained reinforcement learning (RL) made legged locomotion robust well before general manipulation, because walking is cheap to simulate and contact-rich manipulation is not. In 2021 an ANYmal quadruped learned to walk on flat ground in under four minutes, and on uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.before: Legged RL was mainly limited to simulation until Hwangbo and colleagues transferred simulation-trained policies to ANYmal in 2019 <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. Lee and colleagues' proprioceptive controller, trained on much simpler simulated terrain, proved robust in natural environments <Cite id="lee-2020" />. RMA needs no reference trajectories, trains on a terrain generator and deploys on an A1 without fine-tuning <Cite id="rma-2021" />. Radosavovic and colleagues' causal transformer over proprioceptive history carried the recipe to humanoids zero-shot <Cite id="radosavovic-2023" />, and an off-policy recipe now trains humanoid locomotion in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="seo-2025" />.
edits.after: Legged RL left simulation in 2019, when Hwangbo and colleagues transferred trained policies to ANYmal <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. Lee and colleagues' proprioceptive controller then held up in natural environments <Cite id="lee-2020" />, RMA ran on an A1 without fine-tuning <Cite id="rma-2021" />, and an off-policy recipe now trains humanoid locomotion in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="seo-2025" />.

edits.before: Boston Dynamics says RL helps where conditions are easy to simulate but good strategies are hard to describe <Cite id="bd-spot-rl-2024" />.
edits.after: Boston Dynamics says RL helps where conditions are easy to simulate but good strategies are hard to describe <Cite id="bd-spot-rl-2024" />. Rudin and colleagues' policy observes <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term> and 108 terrain-height samples, and a learned network models ANYmal's series-elastic actuators, which are hard to simulate <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Contact-rich manipulation is harder: the 2026 reality-gap survey notes that most simulators assume rigid bodies while real objects deform, that perfect fidelity is computationally infeasible, and that simplified contact models are particularly problematic in contact-rich tasks <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Tang and colleagues blame the cost of physical interaction for RL's difficulty in [robotics](/rl-sim2real/rl-for-robotics) <Cite id="tang-drl-survey-2025" />.

edits.before:
The 2026 reality-gap survey notes that most simulators assume perfectly rigid bodies while real objects deform, and that perfect fidelity is computationally infeasible <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Rudin and colleagues' locomotion policy observes <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term> and 108 terrain-height samples around the base, and because ANYmal's series-elastic actuators are hard to model in simulation, they learn an actuator network <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. For manipulation, the survey says mismatches from simplified contact models are particularly problematic in contact-rich tasks, where precise interaction modeling is crucial <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. It also lists photorealistic rendering among the open sim-to-real challenges <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Tang and colleagues trace RL's difficulty in [robotics](/rl-sim2real/rl-for-robotics) to the cost of interacting with the physical world <Cite id="tang-drl-survey-2025" />.

edits.before: OpenAI's in-hand policy learned finger gaiting without human demonstrations <Cite id="openai-dactyl-2018" />. Its Rubik's-cube policy, trained with automatic domain randomization for a modified Shadow hand, completed one fixed 43-subgoal scramble in two of ten trials with a sensor cube, and zero of ten with vision for face angles <Cite id="openai-rubiks-cube-2019" />. edits.after: OpenAI's in-hand policy learned finger gaiting without human demonstrations <Cite id="openai-dactyl-2018" />. edits.before: AutoMate's generalist solves 20 assemblies and transfers zero-shot <Cite id="automate-2024" />. Play2Perfect reaches 60% on 0.5 mm-clearance insertions zero-shot <Cite id="play2perfect-2026" />. InsertAnything trained one policy only on a simulated hexagonal insertion, and it succeeded on 95.0% of trials across eight unseen real insertion tasks <Cite id="insertanything-2026" />. In simulation, a single insertion world model trained on up to 90 tasks reached 56% zero-shot success on unseen parts, against 7% for a model-free baseline <Cite id="insertion-world-models-2026" />. edits.after: In assembly, AutoMate's generalist solves 20 assemblies zero-shot <Cite id="automate-2024" />, Play2Perfect reaches 60% on 0.5 mm-clearance insertions <Cite id="play2perfect-2026" />, and InsertAnything, trained only on a simulated hexagonal insertion, succeeded on 95.0% of trials across eight unseen real insertion tasks <Cite id="insertanything-2026" />. SPARR's real-world residual adds 38.4% success over zero-shot transfer <Cite id="sparr-2026" />.

edits.before: Such results often need per-task engineering. The cube system used customized hardware, tuned torque limits and a calibrated hand simulation <Cite id="openai-rubiks-cube-2019" />. Zero-shot force-controlled dexterous grasping needed tactile simulation, current-to-torque calibration and actuator models <Cite id="zhao-force-grasp-2026" />. SimToolReal trains one policy over procedural tools that matches specialist policies and transfers zero-shot across 24 real tasks <Cite id="simtoolreal-2026" />. DoorMan's RGB humanoid policy opens doors up to 31.7% faster than teleoperators <Cite id="doorman-2025" />. Boston Dynamics says Atlas learned to lift a fridge with perception done implicitly from proprioception <Cite id="bd-atlas-hard-work-2026" />.
edits.after: Such results often need per-task engineering: zero-shot force-controlled dexterous grasping needed tactile simulation, current-to-torque calibration and actuator models <Cite id="zhao-force-grasp-2026" />. SimToolReal instead trains one policy over procedural tools that transfers zero-shot across 24 real tasks <Cite id="simtoolreal-2026" />, and Boston Dynamics says Atlas learned to lift a fridge with perception done implicitly from proprioception <Cite id="bd-atlas-hard-work-2026" />.

DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 reports 32% to 92% success on multi-finger tasks <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />, and [humanoid whole-body control](/rl-sim2real/humanoid-wbc/) gives its full results.
